title: Cron, and What It Actually Guarantees
description: What a cron expression promises, what it doesn't, and why a scheduled job that looks correct still runs twice or not at all.

learningObjectives.text: Read a five-field cron expression correctly
Name the three things cron does not guarantee
Predict how a scheduling platform's limits change what "daily" actually means

contentSections.title: What the five fields promise, and what they don't

contentSections.body:
You ship a tool that emails a daily summary at 8am. It works for eleven days. On day twelve, three people get the email twice, four minutes apart. On day nineteen, nobody gets it at all, and you only find out because someone asks where it went.

Nothing about your cron expression was wrong. The bug was believing it promised more than it does.

A cron expression is five fields — minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week — and it says exactly one thing: *at these moments, trigger this.* `0 8 * * *` means "at minute 0 of hour 8, every day." `*/15 9-17 * * 1-5` means "every 15 minutes, between 9am and 5pm, Monday to Friday."

That is the whole contract. It says nothing about whether the triggered job finishes, whether it's allowed to still be running when the next trigger fires, or what happens if the platform running the schedule was down at 8:00 and came back at 8:04.

contentSections.problem: Decode `0 */2 * * 1-5` — when does this actually fire?

steps.label: Read the fields left to right
steps.work: minute=0, hour=*/2, day-of-month=*, month=*, day-of-week=1-5
steps.why: Cron fields are always in this order; misreading which field is which is the single most common cron bug.

steps.label: Resolve minute
steps.work: minute 0 — always on the hour, never mid-hour
steps.why: A `0` here rules out anything firing at :15, :30, :45 no matter what the hour field says.

steps.label: Resolve hour
steps.why: The step syntax (`*/N`) divides the full range by N — it does not mean "starting from now, every 2 hours," a very common misreading.

steps.label: Resolve day-of-week
steps.work: 1-5 is Monday through Friday (cron numbers weeks 0=Sunday or 7=Sunday depending on implementation, 1=Monday is consistent everywhere)
steps.why: Weekends are excluded entirely, not just skipped in the hour pattern.

steps.label: State the answer
steps.work: Fires at 00:00, 02:00, 04:00 … 22:00, on weekdays only — 12 times a day, 5 days a week.
steps.why: This is the number that matters for cost: a scheduling platform that bills or rate-limits per invocation cares about 60 invocations a week, not "every 2 hours."

blanks.prompt: What minute does it fire at?
blanks.why: The first field is minute, and it's a fixed value here, not a range or step.

blanks.prompt: What hour?
blanks.why: Also a fixed value — so combined with minute 30, this is a single moment in the day, not a window.

blanks.prompt: Which day(s) of the month?
blanks.why: day-of-month is the third field. A `1` here, combined with `*` for month, means the first day of every month.

blanks.prompt: In one sentence: when does this fire?
blanks.answer: 6:30am on the first day of every month
accept: the first of each month at 6:30am
blanks.why: This is the shape of a "monthly billing summary" job — recognizing it on sight is worth more than being able to write it from scratch.

contentSections.procedure: **Minute → hour → day-of-month → month → day-of-week, left to right, every time.** When two day fields are both restricted (day-of-month *and* day-of-week), most cron implementations fire if *either* matches — which surprises almost everyone the first time they hit it.

contentSections.scenario: A solo builder's "daily digest" tool is scheduled with `0 8 * * *`. On a Tuesday, the platform hosting the scheduler has a five-minute outage starting at 7:58am.
contentSections.question: What happens to that day's 8am trigger?

options.label: It fires at 8:05, once the platform recovers
It fires twice — once queued, once caught up
It depends entirely on the platform — cron itself makes no promise here

feedback.delayed: Some platforms behave this way, but it isn't guaranteed by the cron expression — it's a property of that specific scheduler's recovery behavior, and different platforms make different choices.
feedback.twice: This also happens on some platforms, for the same reason — it isn't what cron promises, it's what that scheduler's queue does with a missed slot.
feedback.depends: Right. The five fields describe *when to trigger*, full stop. Whether a missed trigger is skipped, delayed, retried, or silently dropped is entirely up to the platform running the schedule — Vercel Cron, GitHub Actions, cron-job.org, and a self-hosted crontab on a Linux box all handle this differently, and none of that behavior is visible in the expression itself.

contentSections.concept: **Cron syntax specifies trigger times. It says nothing about delivery, retries, or what happens when the platform running it isn't available at the exact moment.** Reading a cron expression tells you *when* something is supposed to happen. It tells you nothing about whether it reliably does.

contentSections.body: A cron expression is a schedule, not a service-level agreement. Read it for when it fires; look elsewhere for whether it's guaranteed to.

contentSections.title: The three things cron never promised

contentSections.body: Every scheduled-job bug report that starts with "but it's just a cron job, what could go wrong" turns out to be one of exactly three things. Naming them in advance saves the debugging session.

contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in the reasoning, not the config?

options.label: The cron syntax is wrong
"Scheduled" is being treated as synonymous with "reliable"
Vercel Cron doesn't support daily schedules

feedback.syntax: The syntax is fine — `0 8 * * *` correctly means 8:00am daily. The bug isn't in the expression.
feedback.reliable: Right. The config schedules an invocation. It says nothing about whether `/api/send-digest` completes successfully, whether it can be triggered twice, or whether anyone finds out if it stops running — all three of which are genuinely unhandled here. "It's scheduled" and "it's reliable" are different claims, and the gap between them is where this module lives.
feedback.unsupported: Vercel Cron does support this — the config is syntactically and functionally correct as a *trigger*. The gap is in everything after the trigger fires.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This config will genuinely run `/api/send-digest` at 8am every day — that much works. What it does not do is protect against a slow run overlapping the next day's, alert anyone if the function starts erroring, or guarantee the invocation happens at exactly 8:00 rather than 8:00–02 (platform schedulers batch and can have a few minutes of jitter, which most vendors document but nobody reads). Treating a scheduled trigger as a finished feature, rather than the first of four pieces, is the actual defect — and it's a reasoning error, not a config error, which is why it's so common.

contentSections.body:
**1. No guarantee the job finishes.** A trigger firing is not the same as the work completing. If your digest-sending function times out at 10 seconds and takes 14, the platform may kill it mid-send — some recipients got their email, some didn't, and the trigger log says "ran" either way.

**2. No guarantee only one instance runs.** If 8:00's run is still going when 8:00 fires again tomorrow — or, worse, if a platform's own retry logic fires a second invocation because the first one hasn't reported back — you can have two copies of the same job touching the same data at the same time. This is module 1's whole third lesson.

**3. No guarantee you'll know it stopped.** A cron entry with a typo, a job that started throwing an unhandled exception, a schedule quietly disabled by the platform (GitHub Actions disables a scheduled workflow after 60 days with no repository activity, and does not email you) — all of these produce exactly the same symptom: silence. Nothing fires, nothing logs, nobody notices until a user asks.

None of these are edge cases. They are the default behavior of a scheduled job that nobody has specifically hardened against them — which is what the rest of this module is for.
Cron guarantees a trigger time. It says nothing about completion, exclusivity, or whether you'll find out it stopped — harden for all three separately.

title: Serverless Scheduled Functions, Start to Finish
description: Setting up a scheduled function on a platform you don't manage — what you configure, what the platform handles, and what each option actually costs once your tool has real users.

learningObjectives.text: Configure a serverless scheduled function on a real platform
State the free-tier limits and paid costs of at least two scheduling platforms
Choose a scheduling platform against a stated set of constraints

contentSections.title: What you write versus what the platform does

contentSections.body: Ten years ago, "schedule a job" meant SSH-ing into a machine you paid for every month, editing its crontab, and being the person who finds out it's broken when a user complains. Today it can mean a five-line config file and no server at all — as long as you understand what you've traded away to get there.

A serverless scheduled function has two parts: **the function** (ordinary code — a handler that does the work) and **the trigger config** (a platform-specific way of saying "call this on this schedule"). On Vercel, that's a `crons` array in `vercel.json` pointing at an API route. On GitHub Actions, it's a `schedule:` trigger in a workflow YAML file. Both end up doing the same thing: an HTTP request (or a job invocation) arrives on a timer, and your code runs in response.

The function itself doesn't know or care that it was triggered by a schedule rather than a user click — which is exactly why a scheduled endpoint needs its own authentication (more on that in lesson three) rather than trusting that only the scheduler can reach it.

contentSections.intro: You're adding a scheduled function to a Next.js tool deployed on Vercel: check a list of tracked URLs for price drops, once a day, at 6am UTC.

fields.prompt: What does `path` need to point to?
options: A React component
An API route that does the price-check work
A static HTML page
fields.correctValue: An API route that does the price-check work

feedback.A React component: Cron triggers hit an HTTP endpoint, not a rendered UI component — there's no page load happening.
feedback.An API route that does the price-check w: Right — `path` is the URL the scheduler will call, so it needs to be a route with actual handler logic behind it, e.g. `/api/check-prices`.
feedback.A static HTML page: A static page has no server-side code to run, so nothing would actually execute.

fields.prompt: What cron expression fires once daily at 6am UTC?

feedback.6 0 * * *: This fires at 00:06 (six minutes past midnight), not 6:00am — the fields are swapped.
feedback.*/6 * * * *: This fires every 6 minutes, all day — wildly more often than intended, and would quickly hit a plan's invocation limits.

fields.prompt: Vercel Cron schedules always run in which time zone, regardless of your users?
options: The server's local time zone
UTC, always
Whatever time zone the deploying developer is in

feedback.The server's local time zone: Serverless functions don't have a meaningful "local" time zone — they can run in any data center. Vercel standardizes on UTC precisely to avoid this ambiguity.
feedback.UTC, always: Right, and this is worth memorizing rather than looking up each time — it's lesson five's whole subject and the single most common source of "why did this fire at the wrong hour."
feedback.Whatever time zone the deploying develop: It has nothing to do with where you personally are when you deploy — the schedule is evaluated in UTC on Vercel's infrastructure.

contentSections.synthesis: The full entry: `{"path": "/api/check-prices", "schedule": "0 6 * * *"}` inside a top-level `crons` array in `vercel.json`. Three small facts — the path is an endpoint, the schedule is UTC, the syntax is standard cron — and the config is done. The work is all in what `/api/check-prices` does when it's called, which is where the rest of this module lives.

contentSections.body: The trigger config is the easy five minutes. It points a timer at an endpoint — everything that makes the endpoint trustworthy is separate work.

"Just use cron" stops being free advice the moment you check what "free" means on the platform you picked. Every option here has a real limit, and hitting it in production looks like your automation randomly stopping.

contentSections.scenario: A tool needs to run a scraping job every 15 minutes, 24/7, and the builder is on a tight budget.
contentSections.question: Select every statement below that is actually true of the options.

items.label: Vercel Cron on the free Hobby tier can run this schedule as configured
Running this on GitHub Actions in a private repo will consume Actions minutes at a real, budgetable rate
If the repo goes 60 days with no commits, the schedule silently stops firing
Upstash QStash's free tier can absorb this volume indefinitely at zero cost, no matter how it scales
A third-party pinger avoids per-minute billing but adds a dependency the builder doesn't control

explanation.vercelhobby: False as stated — Hobby's minimum interval is once a day. A 15-minute schedule isn't throttled, it's rejected outright when you try to deploy it.
explanation.ghaminutes: True. 96 runs a day, each consuming some slice of the private repo's minute allowance — small individually, real in aggregate, and worth estimating before committing to this approach.
explanation.ghadisable: True, and worth setting a calendar reminder for if the repo is otherwise quiet — a tool that runs fine for two months can go dark with zero code changes.
explanation.qstashfree: False — every free tier has a ceiling. "Indefinitely at zero cost no matter how it scales" describes no real vendor; the free tier buys you a starting point, not a permanent exemption from cost.
explanation.pingerfree: True, and it's the honest trade-off: you've moved the single point of failure from your own infrastructure to a vendor's, which is sometimes the right call and sometimes isn't — the point is knowing you made it.

contentSections.synthesis: There is no free option here that is actually free at this frequency and this reliability bar simultaneously. Every path has a real cost — money, a dependency, or a silent-failure mode — and the honest version of "which should I use" names which cost you're choosing to accept, not which one is magically costless.

contentSections.body:
Three options a solo builder actually reaches for, and what each one costs once you're past a toy project:

**Vercel Cron Jobs.** Free (Hobby) tier: cron jobs are limited to a minimum interval of once per day, and capped at a small number of cron jobs per project — fine for a daily digest, useless for anything that needs to run hourly. The Pro plan removes the once-a-day floor and raises the count, for a monthly seat cost. If your tool needs to check something every 15 minutes, Hobby simply won't let you configure that schedule at all — it's not throttled, it's rejected at deploy time.

**GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger.** Free for public repos; for private repos it draws from your account's included Actions minutes (2,000/month on GitHub Free), and further minutes are billed per-minute past that. The scheduler itself has a real quirk: GitHub queues scheduled workflows and doesn't guarantee they fire at the exact minute — delays of several minutes during high load are normal and documented. And a scheduled workflow is **automatically disabled after 60 days with no commits to the repository**, silently, with no email — the single most common cause of "my GitHub Actions cron just stopped" in the wild.

**A third-party pinger (cron-job.org, Upstash QStash, EasyCron).** These call a URL you provide on a schedule, so your endpoint doesn't need to live on a platform with its own cron feature. cron-job.org is free with generous limits but has no SLA and is a single point of failure you don't control. Upstash QStash has a real free tier (a few hundred messages/day) then charges per message past it — worth it once reliability and delivery guarantees (retries, dead-letter queues) matter more than cost.
Every scheduling platform has a real limit or a real cost. Check it before you build against it, not after a user tells you the automation stopped.

title: What Happens If a Scheduled Run Overlaps the Next One
description: Why a slow run and an on-time trigger can both be active at once, what that actually breaks, and the lock pattern that stops it cheaply.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose symptoms caused by overlapping scheduled runs
Explain why overlap, not just failure, is the dangerous case
Implement a simple lock to prevent concurrent runs of the same job

contentSections.title: The run that's still going when the next one starts

contentSections.body: A nightly job usually finishes in 40 seconds. One night, an upstream API is slow, and it's still running 90 minutes later when the next scheduled trigger fires — right on time, exactly as configured. Now two copies of the same job are reading and writing the same rows.

contentSections.scenario: A tool sends a "weekly report" email once a week, generated by querying a database for the last 7 days of activity and formatting it. One week, subscribers receive two nearly-identical emails, four minutes apart, with slightly different numbers in each.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely mechanism?

options.label: The scheduler fired the trigger twice by mistake
The previous week's run was still finishing when this week's trigger fired, and both ran concurrently against the same data
The email provider sent a duplicate for unrelated reasons

feedback.doubletrigger: Possible in principle on some platforms under specific retry conditions, but the four-minute gap and slightly different numbers point somewhere more specific and more common.
feedback.overlap: Right. If the report-generation query is slow — growing data, a missing index, a slow upstream call — a run can still be mid-query when the next scheduled trigger fires. Nothing stopped it: cron doesn't know or care that yesterday's invocation hasn't finished. Two instances of the same job end up running concurrently, each querying "the last 7 days" at a slightly different moment, which is exactly why the numbers differ.
feedback.provider: Worth ruling out, but it wouldn't explain the numbers being *different* between the two emails — a true provider-level duplicate would send the identical message twice, not two independently-generated ones.

contentSections.mechanism: **Nothing in a standard cron setup prevents two invocations of the same job from running at once.** The scheduler's only job is firing triggers on time; whether the previous invocation has finished is a question it never asks. A job that's usually fast can become an overlap risk the moment its runtime becomes unpredictable — which is most jobs, eventually, as the data they touch grows.

contentSections.body: Overlap is worse than an ordinary failure because both runs *succeed*. There's no error to catch, no exception in a log — just two processes independently doing the same work at almost the same time, which for some jobs is merely wasteful (fetching the same page twice) and for others is actively harmful: two processes both incrementing a counter, both charging a customer, both marking the same batch of rows "processed" and racing on which one's write wins.
Overlap doesn't throw an error — it produces two successful runs touching the same data at once, which is exactly why it's easy to miss.
The fix for overlap isn't making the job faster — you can't guarantee that against every future slowdown. It's making a second concurrent run refuse to start.

contentSections.problem: Add overlap protection to a scheduled function that generates and sends the weekly report.

steps.label: Choose where the lock lives
steps.work: A `job_locks` table with columns `job_name` (unique) and `locked_at`, or a Redis/Upstash key `lock:weekly-report`.
steps.why: The lock has to be somewhere both potential concurrent invocations can see — an in-memory flag in the function itself doesn't work, because each serverless invocation may be a fresh process with no memory of the last one.

steps.label: Try to claim it atomically at the start
steps.work: `INSERT INTO job_locks (job_name, locked_at) VALUES ('weekly-report', now()) ON CONFLICT (job_name) DO NOTHING RETURNING *` — or Redis `SET lock:weekly-report 1 NX EX 600`.
steps.why: "Atomically" is the whole point: if two invocations both check "is it locked?" then both act on the answer, there's a race between the check and the claim. A single atomic operation that both checks and claims in one step closes that gap.

steps.label: If the claim failed, exit
steps.work: If the insert returned no row (or Redis returned nil), another instance already holds the lock — log it and return immediately, doing no work.
steps.why: This is the entire point of the pattern: the second invocation notices it lost the race and gets out of the way instead of doing the work twice.

steps.label: Set a safety expiry
steps.work: The Redis `EX 600` or a scheduled cleanup that deletes locks older than, say, 15 minutes if using a database row.
steps.why: If the job crashes after claiming the lock but before releasing it, an un-expiring lock would permanently block every future run. The expiry has to be comfortably longer than the job's normal runtime, but not so long that a genuine crash blocks things for hours.

steps.label: Release it when done
steps.work: `DELETE FROM job_locks WHERE job_name = 'weekly-report'` or Redis `DEL lock:weekly-report`, in a `finally` block so it runs whether the job succeeded or threw.
steps.why: Releasing in a `finally` (not just after a successful return) is what makes a legitimate failure recoverable on the next scheduled run, rather than compounding into a stuck lock.

faded.problem: Now do the same for a scheduled function that syncs inventory counts from a supplier's API every 15 minutes, using a Postgres `job_locks` table.

blanks.prompt: What SQL claims the lock atomically, assuming a unique constraint on `job_name`?
blanks.answer: INSERT INTO job_locks (job_name, locked_at) VALUES ('inventory-sync', now()) ON CONFLICT (job_name) DO NOTHING RETURNING *
accept: insert into job_locks with on conflict do nothing
blanks.why: Same shape as the worked example — the job name changes, the atomic insert-or-skip pattern doesn't.

blanks.prompt: If that insert returns zero rows, what should the function do?
blanks.answer: log that another instance holds the lock and return immediately without syncing
accept: skip the sync and log it
blanks.why: This is the whole mechanism — losing the race means getting out of the way, not retrying in a loop, which would just hammer the same lock.

blanks.prompt: Given a job that normally takes under a minute but occasionally takes up to 5 on a slow API day, what's a reasonable expiry to guard against a crashed, un-released lock?
blanks.answer: around 10-15 minutes
blanks.why: Comfortably longer than the worst normal case (5 minutes) so a legitimately slow run isn't mistaken for a crash, but short enough that a real crash doesn't block syncing for hours.

blanks.prompt: Where does the lock release happen in the code, and why there specifically?
blanks.answer: in a finally block, so it runs whether the sync succeeds or throws
accept: finally block after success or failure
in a finally so it always runs
blanks.why: A release that only happens on the success path leaves the lock stuck forever the first time the sync throws an error — which, for a job calling an external API, is a when, not an if.

contentSections.procedure: **Claim atomically, exit immediately if the claim failed, expire the lock as a crash safety net, release in a `finally`.** All four matter — skip the atomic claim and you have a race; skip the expiry and a crash locks the job forever; skip the `finally` and the same thing happens on any unhandled error.

contentSections.body:
The pattern is a **lock**: before doing the real work, the job tries to claim a flag that says "I'm running." If the flag is already claimed, it exits immediately instead of doing the work. When it finishes (success or failure), it releases the flag.

The smallest version that actually works: a single row in a database, or a key in a key-value store like Upstash Redis, with an atomic "set if not already set" operation — `SET lock:weekly-report NX EX 600` in Redis terms sets the key only if it doesn't exist, with a 10-minute expiry as a safety net in case the job crashes without releasing it. That expiry matters: a lock with no timeout, held by a job that crashed instead of finishing cleanly, blocks every future run forever.
A lock with an atomic claim, a safety expiry, and a release in `finally` turns "can't happen twice at once" from a hope into a guarantee.

title: Knowing a Scheduled Job Silently Stopped Running
description: Why a scheduled job's failure mode is silence rather than an alarm, and how to build a dead man's switch that notices when nothing happened.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why scheduled-job failures default to silent rather than loud
Design a missed-run alert using a dead man's switch pattern
Evaluate free-tier limits of monitoring services against a real usage pattern

contentSections.title: Why nothing happening looks exactly like nothing happening

contentSections.body: A crashed web server tells you immediately — someone visits, gets an error page, complains within minutes. A scheduled job that stops running tells you nothing. There's no request to fail, no user waiting, no error page. The absence of a log entry looks identical to a quiet day.

This is the structural problem with scheduled work: **its normal state and its broken state produce the same observable evidence — none.** A job that ran and did nothing (because there was nothing to do) looks identical, from the outside, to a job that never ran at all. You cannot tell the difference by *not* looking; you can only tell by building something that actively checks.

The ways a scheduled job goes quiet are mundane: a typo introduced in a config change gets deployed and nobody notices because deploys don't run the cron job as part of the deploy. An API key the job depends on expires. GitHub disables the workflow after 60 days of repo inactivity. The platform has an outage during the exact trigger window. None of these produce a page a user sees, an error a monitoring dashboard defaults to catching, or an email to you — unless you built one.

contentSections.scenario: A tool runs a nightly job that syncs data from a partner API. The job has a `try/catch` around the sync call that logs the error and returns normally if the call fails — written that way so one bad night doesn't crash the whole function. Three weeks later, someone notices the data hasn't updated since a specific date.
contentSections.question: What's actually true about this setup's failure visibility?

options.label: The try/catch means failures are being handled correctly
The try/catch swallows the failure into a log line nobody was watching, which is functionally the same as no error handling at all
This is a scheduling problem, not a code problem

feedback.handled: "Handled" usually implies someone finds out. Catching an error and writing it to a log that nobody reads is functionally silent — the code didn't crash, but the failure is exactly as invisible as if there were no try/catch at all.
feedback.swallowed: Right. Catching the error was the correct instinct — one bad night shouldn't take down the whole function — but catching it and only logging it just moves the silence from "unhandled exception" to "handled exception nobody looked at." The fix isn't removing the try/catch, it's adding an active notification inside the catch block, or a separate monitor that checks whether the sync actually happened recently.
feedback.scheduling: The schedule itself is probably fine — the job is running every night, on time. The problem is entirely about what happens once it runs and fails.

contentSections.concept: **Catching an error and logging it is not the same as knowing about it.** A log is a record you can go read; it is not a notification. The two get conflated constantly, because both feel like "handling" the failure — but only one of them tells you anything before a user does.

contentSections.body: A scheduled job going silent produces no evidence by default. If nothing is actively checking, nobody finds out until a person notices the downstream effect.

The pattern that solves this is inverted from how you'd first guess: instead of the monitor watching for a bad signal from your job, your job has to actively prove it's alive — and the monitor only speaks up when that proof stops arriving.

contentSections.scenario: Healthchecks.io's free tier — a commonly used dead man's switch service — has a real, documented limit on how many checks (i.e. how many distinct scheduled jobs you can monitor) a free account gets.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many checks does the free tier include?
contentSections.explanation: Free tiers on services like this typically sit in the range of a couple dozen checks, which is genuinely enough for a solo builder monitoring several tools' worth of scheduled jobs — the ceiling that actually matters is usually the retention window for ping history (often a few days on free tiers, longer on paid) rather than the check count itself. The number to actually verify before depending on any of this in production is whatever the current pricing page says, since free-tier limits change; the habit that matters is checking it at all, before building the monitor, rather than assuming "free" means "unlimited."

contentSections.body:
A **dead man's switch** (the term comes from train and machinery controls that trigger a stop if the operator's hand releases a lever) works like this: at the end of every successful run, your job pings a monitoring URL — a simple `fetch()` to an endpoint that just needs to receive the request. The monitoring service expects that ping on roughly the same schedule your job runs on, and if the expected ping doesn't arrive within a grace window, *it* alerts you — by email, Slack, SMS, whatever you configured.

The key property: **the alert fires from absence, not from an error your job has to detect and report itself.** If the job crashes before reaching the ping line, times out, gets disabled by the platform, or simply never gets triggered because of a typo in the cron config — all of those look the same to the dead man's switch: the ping didn't arrive, so it says something. You don't have to anticipate every failure mode in your own code, because the monitor doesn't care *why* the ping is missing.

The cost picture, honestly: Healthchecks.io and Cronitor both have real free tiers adequate for a handful of jobs, then paid plans (roughly the price of a coffee subscription per month, scaling with check count and retention) once you're monitoring a real product. The alternative — rolling your own with a database timestamp column and a separate cron job that checks whether it's stale — is free but is itself a scheduled job that can silently stop running, which is the exact problem it exists to solve. This isn't a reason to avoid the DIY approach; it's a reason to put the monitor on infrastructure that's independent of the thing being monitored, which a third-party service gives you for free (in the non-monetary sense) and a second cron job on the same platform does not.
A dead man's switch alerts on absence, not on a detected error — which is what makes it catch failure modes you never thought to code for.

title: Time Zones and the Run That Fires at the Wrong Hour
description: Why almost every scheduling platform runs cron in UTC regardless of your users, and the specific ways "9am" quietly becomes wrong twice a year.

learningObjectives.text: State which time zone a given scheduling platform actually evaluates cron in
Convert a user-facing local time to the correct UTC cron expression
Predict how daylight saving transitions affect a fixed UTC schedule

contentSections.title: "9am" isn't a time until you say whose

contentSections.body: A builder in London sets a cron schedule for `0 9 * * *`, tests it, sees the job fire at 9am on their laptop's clock, and ships it. A user in Los Angeles later asks why their "morning digest" arrives at 1am.

The mistake is assuming a cron expression carries a time zone with it. It doesn't — five numeric fields have no concept of "London" or "local." **The scheduling platform decides which time zone those numbers are evaluated in**, and for essentially every serverless scheduler in common use — Vercel Cron, GitHub Actions, AWS EventBridge by default — that time zone is **UTC**, full stop, regardless of where the developer is, where the servers physically run, or what the platform's dashboard happens to display the current time as.

So `0 9 * * *` fires at 9:00 UTC. In London during British Summer Time (UTC+1), that's 10am local. In Los Angeles during Pacific Daylight Time (UTC−7), that's 2am local. The expression never changes; what it means to a specific user does.

contentSections.scenario: A tool wants a job to fire at 9:00am US Eastern Time. Eastern Time is UTC−5 in winter (EST) and UTC−4 in summer (EDT, daylight saving).
contentSections.question: If the cron expression's hour field is fixed at a single value written today in July, what hour in Eastern local time will 9am UTC-anchored logic actually land on once winter arrives — assuming the developer wrote the expression to hit 9am Eastern *in July*?
contentSections.explanation: In July, Eastern Time is EDT (UTC−4), so 9am Eastern is 13:00 UTC — a cron expression of `0 13 * * *` gets it right in summer. But that expression is a fixed UTC hour; it doesn't know about daylight saving. Once winter arrives and Eastern Time shifts to EST (UTC−5), that same `0 13 * * *` now fires at 8am Eastern, not 9am — the job didn't change, the offset between UTC and the user's local clock did. This is the single most common time-zone bug in scheduled jobs: a schedule tested and confirmed correct in one season quietly drifts by an hour when the clocks change, and nothing in the config or the logs indicates anything happened.

contentSections.body: Cron fields carry no time zone of their own — the platform evaluates them in UTC, and a fixed UTC hour silently drifts against local time whenever daylight saving changes.
There are exactly two honest ways to handle this, and the wrong instinct is a third one that looks reasonable and isn't: manually editing the cron expression by hand twice a year.

contentSections.question: What's wrong with this fix, beyond it being tedious?

options.label: It requires a deploy each time, so it's slow
It depends on a human remembering, on two specific dates, forever — and DST transition dates themselves aren't even fixed calendar dates
vercel.json can't be edited twice a year

feedback.slow: A deploy being required is a minor cost, not the real problem — the deeper issue is what happens the year nobody remembers to make it.
feedback.fragile: Right, and there's a second layer to it: DST transition dates aren't fixed (in the US they're the second Sunday in March and first Sunday in November, which move around the calendar year to year), so even a diligent human following a calendar reminder has to look up the correct date each time rather than trusting a fixed one. A system that depends on a person doing the right manual thing, correctly, on a moving target, twice a year, indefinitely, is not a fix — it's a scheduled failure with a very long fuse.
feedback.cant: There's no technical restriction on editing config twice a year — the problem is entirely about relying on a human to do it correctly and on time, forever.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the exact failure mode of the 'monitoring solves everything' instinct applied to the wrong problem: the schedule doesn't crash or throw, so a dead man's switch won't catch it — the job runs successfully, on time by UTC, just at the wrong local hour. The only real fixes are the two from the lesson: accept UTC and be explicit about it, or compute the local-time correctness in code using a real time zone library rather than a static offset baked into a cron field.

contentSections.body:
**Option one: keep the schedule in UTC, and be explicit that it's UTC.** Fine for internal jobs (nightly database backups, log rotation) where nobody's experience depends on the exact local hour. Document the UTC time in the code and the config, so the next person reading `0 13 * * *` doesn't have to reverse-engineer that it was meant to be 9am Eastern in July.

**Option two: use a platform feature that understands time zones, if one exists.** Some schedulers (certain job queues, some cloud providers' newer cron features) accept an explicit IANA time zone name (`America/New_York`) alongside the cron expression and handle the daylight-saving math for you — firing at 9am local, correctly, across the transition. Check whether your specific platform supports this before assuming it does; Vercel Cron, as of writing, evaluates in UTC only and has no time-zone parameter, which pushes you toward option one or three.

**Option three: compute the correct UTC schedule yourself, in code, using a real time zone library** (like `date-fns-tz` or the built-in `Intl` APIs), rather than a static cron expression. Instead of a fixed schedule, the job runs frequently (say, every 15 minutes) and checks, using proper time zone conversion, whether *right now* corresponds to 9am in the target zone — doing nothing if not. More moving parts, but it's the only approach that's actually correct for a user-facing "send this at 9am your time" feature across DST changes, especially once users are in more than one time zone.
A manual twice-yearly edit is a scheduled failure with a long fuse. Either commit to UTC explicitly, or compute local time correctly in code — never hand-adjust a fixed offset.

title: Practice — Fix Seven Broken Scheduled-Job Setups
description: Seven drills across cron reading, platform limits, overlap, monitoring and time zones. No new concepts — this is where it stops being something you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose scheduled-job failures at speed across the module's five failure modes
Choose the correct fix for a given scheduled-job defect

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or three — nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Add a Monitored Scheduled Job to Your Tool
description: Take a real (or realistic) tool you're building and give it a scheduled job with overlap protection and a missed-run alert — the three pieces this module covered, wired together on one real endpoint.

learningObjectives.text: Configure a working scheduled function on a real platform
Implement overlap protection using an atomic lock
Wire up a dead man's switch that alerts on a missed run

contentSections.body: This is the module's actual point. A scheduled job that can't overlap itself and that tells you when it goes quiet is the difference between an automation you trust and one you're quietly hoping keeps working.

contentSections.title: A scheduled job you'd actually trust
contentSections.brief:
Pick one piece of real, recurring work your tool needs to do — a daily digest, a periodic sync, a nightly cleanup, a scheduled scrape. If you don't have a tool with a natural candidate, use this concrete one: a job that checks a list of tracked URLs (even 2-3 hardcoded ones for the lab) and logs whether their content changed since the last check.

Build the whole path: schedule → lock → work → monitor ping. Each stage below is independently checkable, so a bad day can stop after any of them and leave something real.
contentSections.deliverable: A working scheduled endpoint, deployed and actually firing on its schedule, with an atomic overlap lock and a dead man's switch ping wired into both its success and failure paths.

stages.title: Configure the trigger
stages.instructions: Write the handler function (even if the 'work' is a stub for now) and configure its schedule on your platform — a `vercel.json` crons entry, a GitHub Actions `schedule:` workflow, or an external pinger hitting an authenticated endpoint. Choose a cadence that makes sense for the real work (daily is fine for a lab). Deploy it and confirm, from the platform's own logs, that it fired at least once on schedule.
stages.checkpoint: You can point to a real log entry showing the scheduled trigger fired and reached your code.

stages.title: Add the overlap lock
stages.instructions: Add an atomic claim-or-exit lock at the top of the handler, using whatever storage you have available — a database row with a unique constraint and `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, or a Redis/Upstash `SET … NX EX`. Give it a sensible expiry. Release it in a `finally` block (or equivalent) so both success and failure paths release the lock.
stages.checkpoint: You can explain, specifically, what happens if two invocations of your handler run within the same second — and it isn't 'both do the work.'

stages.title: Wire up the dead man's switch
stages.instructions: Sign up for a monitoring service with a workable free tier (Healthchecks.io is a reasonable default), create a check matching your job's real schedule and a sensible grace period, and add a ping call to your handler's success path. Also decide, deliberately, what happens on the failure path — either skip the ping (so a missed ping correctly signals failure) or ping a separate 'failure' check, and be able to say which you chose and why.
stages.checkpoint: The monitoring service's dashboard shows at least one real ping received from your deployed job, and you can state what happens on its dashboard if the next expected ping doesn't arrive.

rubric.criterion: The scheduled trigger is real and confirmed
rubric.meets: Deployed on an actual platform, with a genuine log entry showing it fired — not just a config file that looks correct.

rubric.criterion: The lock is atomic, not check-then-act
rubric.meets: Uses a single database or Redis operation that both checks and claims, not a separate read followed by a separate write.

rubric.criterion: The lock has a safety expiry
rubric.meets: A crashed run releases the lock on its own within a bounded, stated time — not never.

rubric.criterion: The dead man's switch is genuinely wired in, not just described
rubric.meets: The monitoring dashboard shows at least one real received ping from the deployed job, not a plan to add one.

rubric.criterion: The failure-path decision is explicit and defensible
rubric.meets: You can state, in one sentence, what your handler does on failure with respect to the ping, and why that choice is correct for a missed-run alert to work.

rubric.criterion: The whole thing survives being explained cold
rubric.meets: You could describe schedule → lock → work → ping to someone else without looking at the code, in under two minutes.

contentSections.body: Schedule, lock, work, ping. Four pieces, each one independently the fix for a specific way scheduled jobs quietly fail — and none of them optional if you actually want to trust the thing.

title: Checkpoint — Scheduled Tasks
description: Ten questions pulling across the module. Ungraded, untimed — getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

questions.prompt: What does a cron expression actually guarantee?

options.label: That the job completes successfully
That a trigger fires at the specified times — nothing about completion, exclusivity, or notification
That only one instance of the job can ever run at a time

questions.explanation: The five fields describe when to trigger, full stop. Completion, overlap prevention, and alerting on silence are all separate concerns you have to build.

questions.prompt: What time zone does Vercel Cron (and most serverless schedulers) evaluate cron expressions in?

options.label: The developer's local time zone at the moment of deploy
UTC, regardless of where users or the deploying developer are
Whatever time zone the data center physically running the function is in

questions.explanation: UTC, always, on essentially every major serverless scheduler. A fixed UTC hour will drift against local time whenever daylight saving changes, which is the module's fifth lesson.

questions.prompt: Why is an overlapping scheduled run more dangerous than an ordinary crash?

options.label: Both runs succeed, so nothing throws an error to catch — the damage is silent
Overlapping runs always cost more money in compute
It only affects jobs that write to a database

questions.explanation: Overlap produces two successful runs racing on the same data — no exception, no error log, just two processes doing the same accumulating work (a double charge, a double increment) at once.

questions.prompt: What makes a lock claim 'atomic,' and why does that matter?

options.label: It happens instantly with zero latency
The check-and-claim happen as one database operation, closing the race window a separate SELECT-then-INSERT would leave open
It uses a distributed system rather than a single database

questions.explanation: A check-then-act pattern (SELECT, then decide, then INSERT) has a gap where two near-simultaneous invocations can both pass the check before either claims the lock. A single atomic operation (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, or Redis SET NX) closes that gap.

questions.prompt: Why does a lock need a safety expiry?

options.label: So the lock looks tidy in the database
So a crash between claiming and releasing the lock doesn't block every future run forever
Expiry is required by most database engines for any row

questions.explanation: Without an expiry, a job that crashes after claiming the lock but before releasing it leaves every future scheduled run permanently blocked, since nothing ever clears the lock.

questions.prompt: Why is catching an error and logging it not the same as 'you'll know if it fails'?

options.label: console.error doesn't actually persist logs on serverless platforms
A log is a record someone has to go read; it isn't a notification that reaches anyone
Catch blocks silently swallow all logging calls

questions.explanation: A logged error sits in a stream until someone thinks to check it — which, for a job that normally succeeds silently, could be weeks. Notification requires something that actively reaches you.

questions.prompt: What makes a dead man's switch catch failure modes that error-tracking alone can't?

options.label: It's a faster monitoring approach overall
It alerts on the absence of an expected ping, so it catches failures that prevent your code from running or reporting at all, like a disabled schedule
It doesn't require signing up for a third-party service

questions.explanation: Error tracking needs your code to run far enough to detect and report a problem. A dead man's switch expects a ping and alerts when it's missing, catching things that prevent the code from running at all — a disabled workflow, a config typo, a crash before the ping line.

questions.prompt: A GitHub Actions scheduled workflow that has run fine for months suddenly stops firing, with no code changes. What's a likely cause specific to GitHub Actions?

options.label: GitHub Actions schedules expire after exactly 24 hours by design
GitHub automatically disables a scheduled workflow after 60 days with no commits to the repository, silently
Scheduled workflows require a paid plan after 3 months

questions.explanation: This is a real, documented GitHub Actions behavior and one of the most common causes of a scheduled job silently going dark on that platform — no email, no warning, just a stopped schedule on a quiet repo.

questions.prompt: What's the correct way to handle a 'send at 9am local time' feature for users across multiple time zones?

options.label: Pick one static cron expression tuned to be correct for the average user's zone
Run frequently and check, using a real time zone library, whether it's currently 9am in each user's specific zone
Ask users to manually adjust for their own time zone in the UI

questions.explanation: No single static UTC expression can be '9am local' for users in different zones simultaneously, and a static offset doesn't track daylight saving. A frequent check with real time-zone-aware logic is the only design that's actually correct for this requirement.

questions.prompt: On Vercel's free Hobby tier, what happens if you try to configure a cron job to run every 10 minutes?

options.label: It works but is billed automatically past a threshold
It's rejected — Hobby's minimum interval for cron jobs is once per day
It runs, but only during business hours

questions.explanation: Vercel's Hobby tier caps cron frequency at once daily, enforced at deploy/config time — not a runtime throttle. Anything more frequent requires upgrading, reducing frequency, or triggering the endpoint from an external pinger instead.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: What a Webhook Actually Is, Receiving Side
description: A webhook is an ordinary HTTP request someone else's server sends to yours — which is exactly what makes it useful, and exactly what makes it dangerous to trust by default.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a webhook from polling and explain why each exists
Describe the shape of an inbound webhook request from the receiving side
Identify why an unverified webhook endpoint is a real attack surface

contentSections.body: Your tool creates a Stripe charge. Stripe replies instantly with `status: pending` — the card network hasn't actually cleared it yet. The real answer, succeeded or failed, arrives seconds to minutes later. You have two ways to find out: keep asking, or let Stripe tell you.

contentSections.scenario:
Two integrations, same goal — know when a charge finishes processing.

**A.** A cron job runs every 60 seconds, calling `GET /v1/charges/:id` on Stripe's API and checking the status field.

**B.** Your app registers a URL. When the charge resolves, Stripe's servers send an HTTP POST to that URL with the event details, unprompted.
contentSections.question: Which of these is the webhook?

options.label: A — it's checking status regularly
B — Stripe initiates the request to you
Both — they accomplish the same thing

feedback.a: A is polling — you pulling for an answer on a schedule, whether or not anything changed. It works, but it's wasteful (59 of 60 checks find nothing new) and adds latency (up to 60 seconds of lag by design).
feedback.b: Right. A webhook flips the direction: the other service pushes to you the moment something happens, instead of you repeatedly asking. That's the entire definition — an inbound HTTP request, initiated by someone else's server, arriving at a URL you exposed.
feedback.both: They can reach the same end state, but not the same way, and the difference matters: B has no polling interval to tune, no wasted requests, and near-instant delivery — at the cost of your endpoint needing to be reachable and correct at any moment, unscheduled.

contentSections.concept: **A webhook is push instead of pull.** You register a URL with the other service; when their event happens, their server sends an HTTP request — almost always a POST with a JSON body — to that URL. From your server's perspective, receiving a webhook looks exactly like receiving a request from a browser or a mobile app: an HTTP request arrives, and your code has to decide what to do with it.

contentSections.body:
That last sentence is the one worth sitting with, because it's the source of everything else this module covers. **A webhook endpoint is, mechanically, an ordinary route on your server that anyone on the internet can send a POST to** — not just Stripe, not just the service you registered with. Your code has no innate way to tell "this request really came from Stripe" apart from "this request has a JSON body shaped like a Stripe event," and shaping a fake JSON body is trivial for anyone who's looked at your API docs.

That gap — between *looks like it came from the provider* and *actually came from the provider* — is real, exploitable, and the entire subject of lesson two.

contentSections.question: Put the actual lifecycle of a webhook delivery in order, from the provider's event to your code doing something with it.
steps: An event happens on the provider's side (a charge succeeds, a form is submitted, a deploy finishes)
The provider's server builds a JSON payload describing the event and sends an HTTP POST to your registered URL
Your endpoint receives the request and returns an HTTP status code
Your code (now or shortly after) parses the payload and acts on it — updates a record, sends a notification, whatever the integration needs
contentSections.explanation: The order matters because step 3 and step 4 are not the same step, and treating them as one is where lesson three's whole subject lives — providers expect a fast response at step 3, often within a few seconds, and will consider the delivery failed and retry it if you make them wait for step 4 to finish before responding.

contentSections.body: A webhook is push, not pull — a request the provider sends you, unscheduled, that arrives at your server looking exactly like any other HTTP request. That resemblance is the whole problem this module solves.

contentSections.title: An endpoint the whole internet can reach

contentSections.body: A solo builder ships a `/api/webhooks/stripe` route that reads `req.body.type` and, if it says `checkout.session.completed`, upgrades the user in `req.body.metadata.userId` to Pro. It works in testing. Three weeks later, someone POSTs a hand-crafted JSON body to that exact URL and gets Pro for free, no payment involved.

contentSections.scenario: The route above trusts the request body entirely — if the JSON says the checkout succeeded and names a user ID, the code upgrades that user. There is no other check.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that makes this exploitable?

options.label: The route URL is publicly guessable
The endpoint has no way to distinguish a request Stripe sent from a request anyone else sent
The database doesn't validate the userId field

feedback.url: The URL being guessable or even publicly documented (which webhook URLs often are, by necessity — the provider's dashboard needs it) isn't the vulnerability by itself. Plenty of legitimate, secure endpoints have predictable URLs.
feedback.trust: Right. The URL being known is fine — the problem is that once a request arrives, nothing in the handler asks *is this really from Stripe?* before acting on it. Any POST shaped like a Stripe event is treated as one, regardless of who actually sent it.
feedback.db: The userId being a real, valid ID in the database is exactly what makes this work — the database is doing its job correctly, upgrading a real user. The flaw is entirely upstream of the database, in trusting the request's claim about what happened.

contentSections.mechanism: **An HTTP endpoint has no built-in concept of "who sent this."** A POST request is a POST request; the server sees a method, a path, headers, and a body — nothing that inherently proves origin. Browsers enforce some request restrictions via CORS, but CORS is irrelevant here: nothing stops a script anywhere, run from a terminal, from POSTing directly to a public URL with any body it wants. Proving the request actually came from the provider requires the provider to prove it cryptographically, and requires your endpoint to check that proof before trusting anything in the body — which is exactly what lesson two builds.

contentSections.scenario: A mid-sized SaaS tool integrates with a payments provider and has roughly 2,000 active paying customers. Each customer's billing lifecycle (charges, renewals, disputes, refunds, payment method updates) generates webhook events.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many webhook events might this integration receive in a typical month?
contentSections.explanation: It adds up fast — a single subscription renewal alone can fire several related events (invoice created, payment attempted, payment succeeded, invoice paid), and that's before disputes, updated payment methods, or failed-then-retried charges. The concrete implication: a webhook handler isn't a rarely-invoked path you can afford to leave slow or fragile — at this volume it's closer to a core piece of infrastructure, hit constantly, and every one of this module's failure modes (unverified requests, slow responses, duplicate deliveries) compounds with volume rather than staying a theoretical edge case.

contentSections.body: A webhook endpoint is reachable by anyone, not just the provider. If nothing checks who actually sent the request, the handler will act on whatever anyone sends it.

title: Verifying a Webhook Is Really From Who It Claims
description: How signature verification actually works — a shared secret, an HMAC over the raw body, and a comparison that has to be constant-time to be worth anything.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how HMAC-based webhook signature verification works
Implement signature verification against a raw request body
Identify common implementation mistakes that silently defeat verification

contentSections.title: A secret only you and the provider know

contentSections.body: The fix for "anyone can POST to this URL" isn't making the URL secret. It's making the *request* prove something a forger can't fake — and the mechanism is older and simpler than it sounds.

contentSections.scenario: When you register a webhook endpoint with a provider (Stripe, GitHub, a Slack app), the provider gives you a **signing secret** — a long random string, shown once in their dashboard. Every webhook request the provider sends includes a signature header, computed by running the request body plus that secret through HMAC-SHA256.
contentSections.question: What does verifying that signature actually prove?

options.label: That the request came over HTTPS
That whoever sent this request knows the same secret you were given, and the body wasn't altered in transit
That the request came from the provider's official IP address range

feedback.https: HTTPS protects the request in transit from being read or tampered with by a network eavesdropper — a real and separate protection — but it says nothing about who's on the other end sending the request in the first place. A malicious sender can use HTTPS too.
feedback.hmac: Right. HMAC (hash-based message authentication code) combines the secret with the message in a way that's practically impossible to reproduce without knowing the secret. If you recompute the HMAC using your copy of the secret and it matches the header the request sent, only someone who also has that secret could have produced it — and the provider is the only other party who does.
feedback.ip: Some providers do publish IP ranges as an additional signal, but it's weaker and more brittle than cryptographic verification (ranges change, and IP spoofing exists) — it's not what the signature header is doing, and shouldn't be relied on as the primary check.

contentSections.concept: **HMAC verification proves possession of a shared secret, not identity in the abstract.** You never send your copy of the secret anywhere — you keep it, the provider keeps theirs, and each request lets you check that whoever sent it could compute the same signature you can, which only someone holding the secret can do.

contentSections.body:
The mechanics, concretely, using Stripe's scheme as the example (most providers — GitHub, Slack, Shopify — use a near-identical pattern):

1. The provider computes `HMAC-SHA256(webhook_secret, timestamp + "." + raw_body)` and sends it in a header (`Stripe-Signature`).
2. Your endpoint reads the **raw, unparsed** request body — this matters more than it sounds like it should, covered below — and the timestamp from that same header.
3. Your endpoint recomputes the same HMAC using its own copy of `webhook_secret` (set as an environment variable, never committed to source — treat it exactly like a database password).
4. If your computed signature matches the header's, and the timestamp is recent (within a few minutes, to reject replayed old requests), the request is accepted as genuine.

contentSections.question: This looks correct — it calls the SDK's verification function with the secret. What's actually broken?

options.label: express.json() shouldn't be used at all for any route
JSON.stringify(req.body) re-serializes the already-parsed body, which won't byte-for-byte match what the provider originally signed
The secret should be sent in the request instead of read from an environment variable

feedback.middleware: express.json() is fine for ordinary JSON routes — the problem is specific to webhook verification, which needs the exact raw bytes, not a re-serialization.
feedback.restring: Right, and this is the single most common implementation bug in this lesson's subject. `express.json()` parses the body into a JS object, and JSON.stringify() re-serializes it — but re-serialization isn't guaranteed to produce byte-identical output to the original (key order, whitespace, number formatting can all differ). The signature was computed over the provider's exact original bytes; verifying against a re-stringified approximation will fail for real requests or, worse, only intermittently, which is a much harder bug to catch in testing than a hard failure.
feedback.secret: The secret absolutely should stay server-side, read from an environment variable, never transmitted anywhere — that part of the code is correct as written.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is to capture the raw request body *before* any JSON-parsing middleware touches it — most frameworks provide a way to do this (Express: a raw-body middleware scoped only to the webhook route, run before `express.json()`; Next.js API routes: disable the default body parser for that route and read the raw stream). Verify the signature against those original bytes, and only parse to JSON afterward, once verification has passed.

contentSections.body: Verification checks that whoever sent the request holds the shared secret — and it has to run against the exact raw body bytes the provider actually signed, not a re-parsed approximation.

contentSections.title: Comparing signatures safely, and what it costs to skip this

contentSections.body: Even a correct HMAC computation can be undone by the one line that compares the result — because `===` on two strings leaks information through *how long it takes to return false*, and that's enough for a patient attacker.

contentSections.scenario: A handmade (not SDK) signature check does: `if (computedSignature === headerSignature) { accept() }`. Standard string equality, character by character, stopping at the first mismatch — which is what nearly every language's default `==`/`===` does internally.
contentSections.question: Why do security guides insist on a 'constant-time' comparison here instead of this ordinary one?

options.label: Ordinary comparison is too slow for high webhook volume
Comparing character-by-character and stopping early leaks, via response timing, how many leading characters of a guess were correct — letting an attacker guess the signature one character at a time
JavaScript's === operator doesn't work correctly on strings

feedback.slow: Performance isn't the issue — a 64-character hex comparison is trivially fast either way. The concern is entirely about what an attacker can infer, not about speed.
feedback.timing: Right, and it's a real, exploitable class of attack (a timing attack): if the comparison exits the instant it finds a mismatched character, an attacker who can measure response time precisely enough — and over the internet, with enough repeated attempts and statistics, this is more feasible than it sounds — can incrementally discover the correct signature by noticing which guessed prefix takes marginally longer to reject.
feedback.broken: The operator works exactly as specified — the problem isn't a bug in the language, it's that 'works correctly for general string comparison' and 'is safe for comparing secrets' are different requirements. General comparison is intentionally allowed to short-circuit for speed; secret comparison can't afford that.

contentSections.mechanism: **A constant-time comparison always takes the same amount of time regardless of where (or whether) the strings differ**, so no information leaks through timing. Never hand-roll this — every mainstream language has a built-in for exactly this purpose (`crypto.timingSafeEqual` in Node, `hmac.compare_digest` in Python, `secure_compare` equivalents elsewhere), and every reputable provider's official SDK (Stripe's, GitHub's) already uses it internally in their `constructEvent`/`verify` helper functions — which is the strongest practical argument for using the official SDK's verification function rather than reimplementing HMAC comparison yourself.

contentSections.body: Worth being honest about the actual cost of skipping all of this: it's free. Verification adds no external dependency, no vendor bill — it's a few lines using a library the provider's SDK already ships (`npm install stripe`, already needed for the integration anyway) and one environment variable. There's no budget trade-off here the way there is with, say, a monitoring service's paid tier. The only cost is the ten minutes it takes to wire up correctly, against the alternative of an endpoint that will, eventually, act on a forged request — a free Pro upgrade, a fabricated "payment succeeded" that ships an order that was never paid for, a fake "deploy failed" that pages someone at 3am for nothing.
Use the provider's own SDK to verify — it already gets the raw-body handling and constant-time comparison right, which are the two places a hand-rolled version usually goes quietly wrong.

title: Responding Fast and Doing the Work After
description: Why a webhook handler that does real work before responding gets treated as failed, and how to split acknowledgment from processing without losing anything.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why providers expect a fast response, independent of processing time
Design a handler that separates fast acknowledgment from slower processing
Predict the consequence of an endpoint that regularly times out on the provider's side

contentSections.title: Why 'it worked' and 'I responded fast enough' are different claims

contentSections.body: A webhook handler verifies the signature correctly, then calls three downstream APIs and writes to a database before responding — 4 seconds, usually. Once a month, one of those downstream calls is slow, the handler takes 12 seconds, and the provider marks the delivery as failed and retries it. Now the handler runs the same 4-second sequence twice.

Providers impose a response timeout on webhook deliveries — commonly somewhere around 10-20 seconds depending on the provider, sometimes tighter — and if your endpoint doesn't return an HTTP response within that window, the provider considers the delivery **failed**, not merely slow. Failed deliveries get retried, on a schedule the provider controls, sometimes for hours or days.

This is a completely reasonable design on the provider's side: they have no way to distinguish 'still working on it, give me a minute' from 'crashed and never responding,' so they treat both the same way after the timeout. What it means for you is that **the time your handler takes to fully process an event is directly, and dangerously, coupled to whether the provider thinks the delivery succeeded at all** — and slow processing doesn't just risk a timeout once, it risks a retry storm, since the retried delivery is *also* processed by the same slow code path.

contentSections.problem: A webhook handler for 'order.paid' events currently: verifies the signature, calls the shipping provider's API to create a shipment, calls the tax service to record the sale, updates the order status in the database, and sends a confirmation email — all before responding 200. Split this into a fast-acknowledge path and a processing path.

steps.label: Identify what's actually required before responding
steps.work: Only signature verification and durably recording that the event was received — e.g. inserting a row into an `webhook_events` table with the raw payload and a `pending` status.
steps.why: Everything else (shipping, tax, email) is real work the event triggers, but none of it has to finish before you can honestly say 'I received this.'

steps.label: Respond immediately once that's done
steps.work: Return `200 { received: true }` right after the insert succeeds — typically under 100ms.
steps.why: This is what actually satisfies the provider's timeout. The provider only needs to know you have the event; it has no opinion on when you finish acting on it.

steps.label: Move the real work to an async path
steps.work: After responding (or via a separate queue/background job triggered by the insert), run the shipping call, tax recording, database update, and email send.
steps.why: Decoupling 'acknowledge receipt' from 'do the work' means a slow shipping API on a bad day delays your shipment creation, not your webhook acknowledgment — and doesn't risk the provider marking the whole delivery failed.

steps.label: Track completion, not just receipt
steps.work: Update the `webhook_events` row's status to `processed` (or `failed`, with an error) once the async work finishes — giving you a queryable record of what's actually been handled versus what's stuck.
steps.why: Without this, 'I responded 200' and 'I actually did the work' get conflated again, just one layer deeper — you need visibility into whether the async step itself succeeded.

faded.problem: Now apply the same split to a 'form.submitted' webhook from a form-builder tool, whose handler currently verifies the signature, then synchronously calls an AI API to summarize the response, posts the summary to Slack, and appends a row to a spreadsheet — all before responding.

blanks.prompt: What are the only two things that need to happen before responding 200?
blanks.answer: verify the signature and durably record that the event was received
accept: verify signature and store the event
signature check and persist the event
blanks.why: Same principle as the worked example — acknowledgment requires proof of receipt, not proof of completed processing.

blanks.prompt: Which three operations move to the async/background path?
blanks.answer: the AI summary call, the Slack post, and the spreadsheet append
accept: summarize, post to slack, append to spreadsheet
blanks.why: All three are genuine downstream work triggered by the event, none of which the provider needs completed to consider the delivery successful.

blanks.prompt: Why is moving the AI summary call specifically important here, beyond general speed?
blanks.answer: AI API calls have unpredictable, sometimes multi-second latency, making them one of the likeliest single causes of a timeout if left in the synchronous path
accept: LLM calls are slow and variable, a common timeout cause
blanks.why: This is a concrete, track-relevant instance of the general principle — any call whose latency you don't fully control is a timeout risk if it sits between request and response.

blanks.prompt: What should track whether the async summary-to-Slack-to-spreadsheet chain actually completed?
blanks.answer: a persisted status field on the stored event record, updated once the chain finishes or fails
accept: a status column updated after processing
an event record with a processed/failed status
blanks.why: Same as the worked example's last step — fast acknowledgment buys you nothing if you then have no way to know whether the real work quietly failed afterward.

contentSections.procedure: **Verify, persist, respond — then process.** The first three have to happen fast and in that order; everything the event actually triggers happens after, tracked separately, so a slow downstream call never threatens the provider's view of whether the delivery succeeded.

contentSections.body: The provider's timeout measures how fast you acknowledge, not how fast you finish. Persist the event and respond immediately; do the real work after, tracked separately.

contentSections.title: What actually happens when this goes wrong

contentSections.body: "Just make the handler faster" is not always available to you — sometimes the slow part is a downstream API you don't control. What you can always control is where the slow part sits relative to the response.

contentSections.scenario: A tool's webhook handler synchronously calls a third-party enrichment API (looks up company data for a new signup) before responding. That API has a p99 latency of 8 seconds and, once or twice a week, hangs for over 20 seconds. The provider's dashboard shows a rising count of 'failed' deliveries for this endpoint, and support tickets mention duplicate welcome emails.
contentSections.question: What's the causal chain connecting the slow API call to duplicate emails?

options.label: The enrichment API itself is sending duplicate requests
Slow responses cross the provider's timeout, the provider marks the delivery failed and retries it, and the retried delivery runs the same handler (including the welcome email) again
The database is duplicating rows due to a missing unique constraint

feedback.enrichment: The enrichment API being slow is the trigger, but it isn't itself sending anything twice — it's just taking too long, which sets the rest of the chain in motion.
feedback.retry: Right. This is the whole chain from this lesson connected end to end: slow synchronous work → response arrives too late → provider's timeout treats the delivery as failed → provider retries → the retried request re-runs the entire handler, welcome email included, because nothing distinguishes 'first delivery of this event' from 'a retry of the same event.'
feedback.db: A missing unique constraint could be a contributing factor to why the *database* ends up with duplicate rows, but it doesn't explain the duplicate *emails* being sent — that's a retry-triggered re-execution, not a database-layer issue.

contentSections.mechanism: **A timeout doesn't just fail silently — it triggers exactly the retry behavior a provider is supposed to have, working correctly, against a handler that isn't ready for it.** This is also why lesson three and lesson four are connected: making the handler fast enough to avoid unnecessary retries reduces how often duplicates happen, but doesn't eliminate the need to handle duplicates safely — retries are a legitimate, expected part of the webhook contract, not just a failure mode to prevent outright.

contentSections.body: One more honest cost to name: moving work to a background/async path is itself infrastructure. A simple version might be "respond, then continue executing after the response is sent" (works on a long-running server; on some serverless platforms, code after the response can be killed once the response is flushed, so check your platform's actual guarantee here). A more robust version uses a real queue — Vercel's own queueing primitives, a lightweight job library backed by Redis, or a message queue service — which adds a dependency and, past its free tier, a real cost that scales with volume. For a solo builder's first webhook integration, persisting the event and processing it in a `setImmediate`/background continuation is often good enough; the queue is worth the added cost and complexity once retries, ordering, or processing failures need to be handled with more care than 'try again next time.'

A timeout isn't a dead end — it's the provider correctly doing its job (retrying) against a handler that wasn't built to expect it. Fast acknowledgment reduces retries; it doesn't remove the need to survive them.

title: Idempotency: The Webhook That Arrives Twice
description: Why duplicate delivery is a normal, expected part of the webhook contract rather than a rare failure, and the event-ID pattern that makes handling it cheap.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why at-least-once delivery makes duplicates a routine occurrence
Implement idempotent event handling using a stored event-ID check
Distinguish operations that are naturally idempotent from ones that need explicit protection

contentSections.title: Twice isn't a bug in the provider

contentSections.body: A support ticket: "I got charged twice for the same order, and I only clicked Pay once." The webhook handler that increments the paid-order count doesn't check whether it's already seen this specific event before — and the provider sent it twice, exactly as its own documentation says it might.

Most webhook providers document their delivery guarantee as **at-least-once**, not exactly-once — meaning they'll make sure you get the event *at least* one time, and will re-send it if they're not confident you received it, even if you actually did. From the provider's side this is the safer failure mode: better to risk a duplicate than risk you silently missing a payment confirmation. From your side, it means **duplicate delivery isn't an edge case to defend against — it's a documented, routine part of the contract**, and a handler that assumes 'each event arrives exactly once' is building on a premise the provider explicitly does not promise.

contentSections.scenario: Here are situations that can cause the same webhook event to be delivered to your endpoint more than once.
contentSections.question: Select every one of these that is a real, documented cause of duplicate delivery — not just a theoretical possibility.

items.label: Your handler responded after the provider's timeout, triggering an automatic retry
The provider's platform simply guarantees at-least-once delivery as a design choice, independent of any failure
Someone with dashboard access manually clicked 'resend' on a past event
The user's browser tab was refreshed while viewing a page
A network blip caused the provider's own retry logic between its internal systems to re-send

explanation.timeout: Directly covered in lesson three — a slow response looks identical to a failure from the provider's side, and triggers its retry policy.
explanation.atleastonce: This is the important one to internalize: it's not a failure mode at all from the provider's perspective, it's the guarantee working as designed. Even a perfectly healthy, fast, always-online endpoint can receive duplicates under this model.
explanation.manual: A completely mundane, everyday cause — most provider dashboards expose a 'resend' button precisely for debugging, and it's used more often than builders expect.
