explanation.browser: A user's browser behavior has no connection to whether the provider re-sends a webhook to your server — this is a client-side action entirely unrelated to the provider-to-server delivery.
explanation.networkflake: Real and outside your control — the provider's own infrastructure can have transient issues that trigger their internal retry logic, resulting in what looks, from your side, like the same event arriving twice.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these are exotic. A dashboard resend and a provider's own documented at-least-once guarantee are both completely ordinary, expected events — not obscure failure scenarios. Building a handler that can't tolerate a duplicate isn't a handler with a rare edge-case gap; it's a handler that will demonstrably misbehave in production, on a schedule outside your control.

contentSections.body: At-least-once delivery means duplicates are a documented feature of the contract, not a failure to eliminate. Build for them from the start.
The fix doesn't require detecting that two requests are 'the same' by comparing their contents — every webhook event already comes with exactly the identifier you need.

contentSections.intro: Design an idempotent webhook handler for a 'checkout.session.completed' event that fulfills an order exactly once.

fields.prompt: Where should processed event IDs be tracked?
options: In an in-memory array in the server process
In a persistent store — a database table with a unique constraint on event ID
Nowhere — check the order's current status instead
fields.correctValue: In a persistent store — a database table with a unique constraint on event ID

feedback.In an in-memory array in the server proc: Serverless functions and most modern deployments don't guarantee the same process handles the next request — an in-memory array resets or is inconsistent across invocations, so this doesn't actually protect anything reliably.
feedback.In a persistent store — a database table: Right — a `processed_webhook_events` table with a unique constraint on `event_id` gives you both a durable record and, if you use an atomic insert, a race-safe check in one step.
feedback.Nowhere — check the order's current stat: This can work for some cases but is weaker and more error-prone than tracking the event ID directly — the order's status might legitimately change between a first and second delivery for unrelated reasons, giving false signals either way.

fields.prompt: How should the handler check whether it's already processed this event?
options: Compare the new event's full payload byte-for-byte against the last one received
Attempt to atomically insert the event ID into the tracking table; if the insert fails due to the unique constraint, it's a duplicate
Ask the provider's API whether this event was already acknowledged
fields.correctValue: Attempt to atomically insert the event ID into the tracking table; if the insert fails due to the unique constraint, it's a duplicate

feedback.Compare the new event's full payload byt: Comparing content is fragile and unnecessary — the event ID already exists specifically to make this comparison trivial and exact, without touching the payload at all.
feedback.Attempt to atomically insert the event I: Right — this is the same atomic-claim pattern from the overlap-lock lesson in module one, applied to a different problem: one database operation that both checks and claims, closing the race window a separate SELECT-then-INSERT would leave open.
feedback.Ask the provider's API whether this even: This adds an unnecessary external dependency and round-trip for information you can track yourself, locally, for free.

fields.prompt: If the event ID is already present (a genuine duplicate), what should the handler do?
options: Return an error status so the provider knows something's wrong
Return the same success response as a first-time delivery, and skip the fulfillment logic entirely
Re-run the fulfillment logic anyway, since it's probably safe
fields.correctValue: Return the same success response as a first-time delivery, and skip the fulfillment logic entirely

feedback.Return an error status so the provider k: Nothing is actually wrong here — a duplicate delivery under an at-least-once guarantee is expected, healthy behavior. Returning an error would likely trigger yet another retry of an event that's already been handled correctly.
feedback.Return the same success response as a fi: Right — from the provider's perspective, this delivery should look exactly as successful as the first one. The only difference is your handler quietly does nothing further, because the order was already fulfilled.
feedback.Re-run the fulfillment logic anyway, sin: This is precisely the assumption that causes double-charges and duplicate shipments — 'probably safe' isn't good enough for an operation with a real-world side effect.

contentSections.synthesis: The full pattern: on every event, atomically try to insert its ID into a tracking table. If the insert succeeds, this is the first time you've seen it — proceed with fulfillment. If it fails on the unique constraint, this is a duplicate — return success anyway, and do nothing further. The provider sees a healthy 200 either way; your fulfillment logic runs exactly once no matter how many times the same event arrives.

contentSections.body: Every well-designed webhook payload includes a **unique event ID** — Stripe's events have an `id` field like `evt_...`, GitHub's deliveries include an `X-GitHub-Delivery` header, and so on. That ID is stable across retries: a resent delivery of the same event carries the *same* ID, not a new one. This is the whole mechanism idempotent handling relies on.

Every well-designed event carries a stable ID across retries. An atomic insert-or-detect-duplicate check against that ID makes fulfillment run exactly once, no matter how many times the delivery repeats.

title: Testing Webhooks Locally Without Deploying Every Time
description: How to get real webhook events onto your laptop during development — a tunnel to expose localhost, and a CLI that can replay real event payloads on demand.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why webhook development needs a publicly reachable URL even during local development
Use a tunneling tool to receive real webhook deliveries on a local machine
Choose between a tunnel and a provider's CLI-based event simulator for a given testing need

contentSections.body: The obvious way to test a webhook handler — run it locally, register `http://localhost:3000/webhooks` with the provider — doesn't work, and the reason is worth understanding rather than just working around: the provider's servers are somewhere on the internet, and `localhost` on your laptop means nothing to them. It resolves, on their machine, to their own machine, not yours.

contentSections.scenario: A builder is developing a webhook handler and needs to see real events arrive while running the server on their own laptop, before deploying anything.
contentSections.question: What has to be true for the provider's webhook delivery to actually reach the developer's local machine?

options.label: Nothing extra — any URL, including localhost, works as long as it's typed correctly
The developer's local server needs to be reachable via some publicly routable URL, even temporarily
The provider needs to be told the developer's home IP address directly

feedback.nothing: localhost is meaningful only on the machine it's typed on — it's a loopback address, not a real network destination anyone else's server can reach. This is true regardless of how correctly it's typed.
feedback.tunnel: Right. Something has to bridge the gap between 'a public URL the provider can send an HTTP request to' and 'a process running on a laptop behind a home or office router, usually without a static public IP or open inbound ports at all.' That bridge is what a tunneling tool provides.
feedback.ip: Even with a known IP, most home and office networks don't route inbound traffic to a specific machine by default (NAT, firewalls, no port forwarding configured) — this would require real network configuration most developers neither have nor want to set up just for testing.

contentSections.concept: **A tunneling tool creates a temporary public URL that forwards incoming requests to a port on your local machine.** ngrok is the best-known example; Cloudflare Tunnel and a few others offer similar functionality. Run `ngrok http 3000`, get back a URL like `https://a1b2c3.ngrok-free.app`, register *that* URL with the provider (or its dashboard's test-webhook feature) instead of localhost, and real webhook deliveries now reach your laptop.

contentSections.body: The cost picture: ngrok's free tier gives you a working tunnel with a randomly-generated URL that changes every time you restart it — fine for a single dev session, mildly annoying if you need to re-register the URL with the provider each time. A paid plan (a modest monthly fee) buys a fixed subdomain so the URL doesn't change, which matters once you're testing against a webhook config you don't want to re-enter constantly. Cloudflare Tunnel is free with a Cloudflare account and, unlike ngrok's free tier, doesn't rotate the URL on restart if configured with a named tunnel — a genuinely good zero-cost option once you're past the five-minute quick-start.
localhost is invisible to the internet by design. A tunnel gives the provider a real public URL that forwards to your local machine, which is what makes local webhook testing possible at all.

contentSections.title: Replaying events without waiting for the real thing

contentSections.body: A tunnel gets real events to your laptop — but waiting for a real payment dispute to happen, just to test how your handler processes a `charge.dispute.created` event, is a terrible way to spend a Tuesday.

contentSections.question: What's the real problem with this approach, beyond it being extra manual work?

options.label: curl isn't a reliable enough tool for this
It tests a hand-guessed payload shape with no signature, so it silently never exercises the actual verification code path or catches a payload-shape mistake
Local testing should never use fake data at all

feedback.curl: curl works fine as a tool — the problem isn't the tool, it's what's being sent through it.
feedback.guessed: Right, and it's two separate problems stacked: first, a hand-guessed payload can easily miss real fields, nested structures, or edge cases the actual provider includes — bugs that only surface against genuine data. Second, skipping the signature header means the verification code from lesson two never actually runs during this test, so a broken verification check could ship unnoticed, having never been exercised by anything except real production traffic.
feedback.nofake: Fake or synthetic data isn't inherently the problem — a provider's own official event simulator (covered next) generates synthetic events too. The issue is specifically *hand-guessed, unsigned* data standing in for something that should be realistic and properly signed.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Most major providers ship a CLI specifically to solve this — the Stripe CLI, for one, can forward real webhook events to a local port (`stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhooks`, which itself acts as a tunnel *and* handles signing) and can also trigger synthetic test events on demand (`stripe trigger charge.dispute.created`) using its own test-mode data, correctly signed with a CLI-specific webhook secret. This gets you both realistic payload shapes and a genuine signature to verify against, without waiting for a real event or hand-authoring one.

contentSections.body: The practical choice between a general tunnel and a provider's own CLI: if the provider has a CLI with event forwarding and triggering built in (Stripe, and increasingly others follow this pattern), prefer it — it's free, and it solves both the tunneling problem and the signature problem at once, using data shaped exactly like production. Reach for a general tunnel like ngrok when the provider doesn't offer this, or when you need to receive genuinely real (not simulated) events during development — testing against an actual third-party integration's live sandbox environment, for instance, where a CLI's synthetic test events wouldn't be representative enough.

Prefer a provider's own CLI when one exists — it tunnels and signs correctly at once, using realistic data. Reach for a general tunnel like ngrok when no such CLI exists or you need genuinely live events.

title: Practice — Fix Seven Insecure or Fragile Webhook Handlers
description: Seven drills across verification, speed, idempotency and testing. No new concepts — this is where it stops being something you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose insecure or fragile webhook handlers at speed
Choose the correct fix among the module's four hardening patterns

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or three — nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Add a Verified, Idempotent Webhook Handler
description: Build a real webhook endpoint end to end: verified against a raw body signature, responding fast, and safe against duplicate delivery — tested locally before it ever touches production.

learningObjectives.text: Implement signature verification against a raw request body using a provider's SDK
Separate fast acknowledgment from slower event processing
Implement idempotent handling using an atomic event-ID check

contentSections.body: This is the module's whole point assembled into one endpoint. A webhook handler that rejects forgeries, answers fast, and shrugs off duplicates is the difference between an integration you trust and one you're quietly hoping behaves.

contentSections.title: A webhook handler you'd actually trust
contentSections.brief:
Pick a real provider your tool integrates with (or could) that sends webhooks — a payments provider, a form tool, a deploy platform, a chat integration. If nothing fits, use this concrete stand-in: build a `/api/webhooks/test` endpoint and a small local script that sends it correctly-signed events using a shared secret you generate yourself, simulating a real provider's behavior closely enough to exercise every stage below.

Build the whole path: verify → persist → respond → process async → survive a duplicate. Each stage is independently checkable.
contentSections.deliverable: A working webhook endpoint, deployed and reachable, that rejects unsigned or incorrectly-signed requests, responds within a few hundred milliseconds, and produces the same correct end state whether a given event is delivered once or three times in a row.

stages.title: Verify the signature against the raw body
stages.instructions: Set up the route with the body-parsing middleware disabled or bypassed for this path, capture the raw bytes, and verify the signature using the provider's SDK (or your own HMAC-SHA256 comparison using a constant-time compare function, if building the test stand-in). Confirm, concretely, that an unsigned or badly-signed request is rejected — actually send one and watch it fail.
stages.checkpoint: You can send a request with a deliberately wrong signature and watch the handler reject it, and a genuinely correct one and watch it pass.

stages.title: Persist and respond fast
stages.instructions: Insert a row recording the event (its ID, type, and raw payload) into a table, then respond 200 immediately — before any of the 'real' work for this event runs. Time it: it should be well under a second, ideally under 200ms.
stages.checkpoint: You can point to a timestamp or log showing the response returned before any downstream processing began.

stages.title: Move real processing to an async path
stages.instructions: Add whatever the event should actually trigger — for the test stand-in, something simple like logging a formatted summary or writing a second derived record is fine — and run it after the response has been sent, not before.
stages.checkpoint: You can explain, specifically, what would happen to the response time if this processing step suddenly took 10 seconds — and confirm it wouldn't be anything.

stages.title: Add the idempotency check and prove it
stages.instructions: Add the atomic event-ID check from lesson four: attempt to insert the event ID with a unique constraint, and skip processing entirely if that insert fails. Then actually test it — send the exact same signed event twice (or three times) and confirm the processing step (the log line, the derived record) only happened once, while both requests still received a 200.
stages.checkpoint: You have direct evidence — a log, a query result — that the same event delivered multiple times produced the same end state as delivering it once.

rubric.criterion: Verification is real and demonstrated, not assumed
rubric.meets: You've actually sent both a valid and an invalid signature and observed the correct accept/reject behavior — not just written code you believe is correct.

rubric.criterion: Verification uses the raw body, not a re-parsed one
rubric.meets: The signature check runs against bytes captured before any JSON-parsing middleware touched them.

rubric.criterion: The response is genuinely fast
rubric.meets: Response time is measured, not assumed, and stays well under any reasonable provider timeout even while downstream processing is deliberately slow.

rubric.criterion: Duplicate handling is atomic, not check-then-act
rubric.meets: Uses a single insert-with-unique-constraint operation, not a separate SELECT followed by a separate INSERT.

rubric.criterion: Idempotency is proven with a real duplicate send, not just described
rubric.meets: You have concrete evidence the same event sent multiple times produced the processing effect exactly once.

rubric.criterion: The whole path survives being explained cold
rubric.meets: You could describe verify → persist → respond → process → dedupe to someone else without looking at the code, in under two minutes.

contentSections.body: Verify, persist, respond, process, dedupe. Five pieces, each the fix for a specific way webhook handlers quietly fail — and the only way to know they work is to actually send a forged request and a duplicate one and watch what happens.

title: Checkpoint — Webhooks
description: Ten questions pulling across the module. Ungraded, untimed — getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

questions.prompt: What is a webhook, structurally?

options.label: A scheduled request your server sends to check for updates
An HTTP request another service's server sends to a URL you exposed, when an event happens on their side
A persistent connection kept open between two servers

questions.explanation: A webhook is push, not pull — the provider initiates an HTTP request to you, unscheduled, the moment their event occurs. From your server's perspective it looks exactly like any other inbound HTTP request.

questions.prompt: Why can't a webhook endpoint trust an incoming request just because it's shaped like a real event from the provider?

options.label: HTTP requests can't carry JSON bodies reliably
The endpoint is an ordinary URL anyone can POST to — nothing about the request's shape proves who actually sent it
Providers deliberately randomize their payload structure

questions.explanation: An HTTP endpoint has no built-in concept of sender identity. A forged request with a correctly-shaped JSON body looks identical to a genuine one unless something — a cryptographic signature — proves origin.

questions.prompt: What does verifying an HMAC signature actually prove?

options.label: That the request used HTTPS
That whoever sent the request knows the same shared secret you were given, and the body wasn't altered
That the request came from the provider's official IP range

questions.explanation: HMAC verification proves possession of a shared secret. Since only you and the provider hold that secret, a matching signature means the request genuinely came from the provider (or leaked-secret access, which is why the secret has to be protected like a password).

questions.prompt: Why does signature verification have to run against the raw, unparsed request body?

options.label: Raw bodies are faster to process
The provider signed the exact original bytes — a re-serialized version of the parsed body isn't guaranteed to match byte-for-byte
Parsed JSON objects can't be hashed at all

questions.explanation: Re-serializing an already-parsed body (via JSON.stringify or similar) doesn't reliably reproduce the provider's original bytes — differences in key order, whitespace, or number formatting can silently break verification against real requests.

questions.prompt: Why must signature comparison be constant-time rather than a standard string equality check?

options.label: Standard equality is too slow for high-volume endpoints
A comparison that exits early on the first mismatched character leaks, via response timing, how many leading characters were guessed correctly
Standard equality doesn't work correctly on hash strings

questions.explanation: A timing attack exploits early-exit comparison behavior to reconstruct a secret one character at a time via measured response timing. Constant-time comparison always takes the same time regardless of where a mismatch occurs, closing that leak.

questions.prompt: What does a provider's webhook response timeout actually measure?

options.label: Whether your handler's internal processing eventually completes successfully
How long it takes your endpoint to return an HTTP response, regardless of whether downstream processing is still running
The total time your server has been running without restarting

questions.explanation: The provider only sees whether an HTTP response arrived within its window. It has no visibility into your internal processing — a handler that's still working but hasn't responded is treated identically to one that's crashed.

questions.prompt: What's the correct split for a webhook handler with slow downstream work (emails, third-party API calls)?

options.label: Do all the work synchronously, and just accept occasional timeouts
Verify and persist the event, respond immediately, then run the slower work asynchronously afterward
Skip persisting the event and rely on the provider to resend it if something goes wrong

questions.explanation: Only verification and durable receipt need to happen before responding. Everything the event triggers as a consequence belongs in an async path, so its latency can't threaten the response timeout.

questions.prompt: What does 'at-least-once delivery' mean for how a webhook handler should be built?

options.label: Duplicate events are a rare edge case worth a quick defensive check
Duplicate delivery is a routine, documented part of the contract, and the handler must be idempotent from the start
The provider guarantees exactly one delivery per event under normal conditions

questions.explanation: At-least-once is a deliberate design choice many providers make, favoring occasional duplicates over any risk of a missed event. It means duplicate delivery is expected, ordinary behavior, not a rare failure to shrug off.

questions.prompt: What makes the event-ID check pattern (attempt an atomic insert, treat a unique-constraint failure as a duplicate) safer than a SELECT-then-INSERT check?

options.label: It uses less database storage
It closes the race window where two near-simultaneous deliveries could both pass a SELECT check before either has recorded the event
It doesn't require a database at all

questions.explanation: A check-then-act pattern has a gap between checking and recording where two near-simultaneous deliveries can both see 'not yet processed' and both proceed. A single atomic insert closes that gap — the same principle as the overlap lock from module one.

questions.prompt: Why can't a webhook provider's servers reach an endpoint registered as http://localhost:3000 during local development?

options.label: localhost is a loopback address, meaningful only on the machine it's used on — the provider's servers have no route to your laptop
Most providers technically block the word 'localhost' in URLs
Port 3000 is reserved and can't receive external traffic

questions.explanation: localhost always resolves to 'this machine' — on the provider's own servers, that points back to themselves, not to your laptop. A tunneling tool (or a provider's own CLI with forwarding built in) bridges this gap with a temporary public URL.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Incoming Webhooks Versus a Real Slack App
description: Two genuinely different ways to post into Slack — a five-minute URL versus a registered app — and which one a given tool actually needs.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what an incoming webhook URL can and can't do in Slack
Explain what a Slack app adds beyond an incoming webhook
Choose the right integration path for a given tool's requirements

contentSections.body: A solo builder wants their nightly scraping tool to post a summary in #alerts. The whole integration turns out to be one URL and one HTTP POST — no app review, no install flow, nothing a Slack admin has to approve. That's not a shortcut; it's the entire feature.

contentSections.scenario: Slack's **Incoming Webhooks** feature: a workspace admin (or anyone with permission) creates a webhook for a specific channel from Slack's own settings, gets back a unique URL like `https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXXX`, and any tool that POSTs a JSON payload to that URL gets a message posted into that channel.
contentSections.question: What does that URL actually authorize?

options.label: Posting messages to any channel in the workspace
Posting messages to the one specific channel it was created for, nothing else
Reading messages from the channel as well as posting

feedback.any: An incoming webhook is scoped to a single channel at creation time — it has no ability to post anywhere else, which is a deliberate, narrow permission.
feedback.one: Right. The URL is a one-way, single-channel capability: anyone who has it can post a message into that specific channel, and that's the entire surface area. Nothing about reading, reacting, or acting anywhere else in the workspace.
feedback.read: Incoming webhooks are write-only in a real sense — POST a message, that's the whole interaction. There's no read capability, no way to see channel history or list users, through this mechanism.

contentSections.concept: **An incoming webhook is a bearer-token URL scoped to exactly one channel and exactly one action: post a message.** Whoever holds the URL can post there — there's no further authentication — which is why it should be treated as a secret exactly like an API key, not pasted into a public repo or a shared doc.

contentSections.body: The payload itself is deliberately simple JSON: `{"text": "Nightly scrape finished: 42 new listings found."}` POSTed to the webhook URL is enough to produce a message. Slack also accepts a richer structure — `blocks`, covered in the next lesson — for formatting beyond plain text. That's essentially the entire API surface: no OAuth flow, no bot user, no scopes to request, no Slack app to register at all.

contentSections.scenario: A builder is deciding whether an incoming webhook is enough for their tool's Slack integration.
contentSections.question: Select every requirement below that an incoming webhook genuinely cannot satisfy on its own.

items.label: Post a formatted summary message into one specific channel
Let each user of the tool choose which of several channels their own results post to, without an admin creating a new webhook for each one
Read replies users post in the thread under the bot's message and react to them
Include headers, dividers, and structured sections in the message
Post as a distinct, named bot user with its own avatar that users can DM directly

explanation.postone: This is exactly what an incoming webhook is built for — posting a formatted message to its one configured channel.
explanation.multichannel: A webhook URL is bound to one channel at creation. Supporting user-chosen destinations without per-user admin setup needs a real Slack app with OAuth, so each user can install it and pick their own channel — this module's lesson five.
explanation.readreply: Incoming webhooks are write-only. Reading anything back — replies, reactions, message history — requires a Slack app with the relevant read scopes and, typically, the Events API.
explanation.richformat: Slack's Block Kit (headers, dividers, sections, buttons) works over an incoming webhook exactly as well as it does through a full app — formatting richness isn't the differentiator here.
explanation.botidentity: A webhook message posts under a generic name you can override per-message, but it isn't a persistent, DM-able bot identity — that requires a registered Slack app with a bot user.

contentSections.synthesis: The line isn't about formatting quality — both paths can look equally polished. It's about **anything requiring identity, reading, or per-user configuration**. A webhook posts to one fixed destination and nothing more; the moment a tool needs to read Slack, act as a persistent bot, or let end users choose their own channel, that's a real Slack app, not a webhook.

contentSections.body: An incoming webhook is a single-channel, write-only, no-setup URL. It's genuinely enough for most solo tools — until a feature needs reading, bot identity, or per-user destinations.

contentSections.title: What a real Slack app actually adds

contentSections.body: A tool grows a feature: "let each customer connect their own Slack workspace and choose their own channel." The incoming webhook approach — hand each customer a URL to paste in — technically works and is also a support nightmare and a real security smell. This is where the extra setup starts paying for itself.

contentSections.scenario: A SaaS tool with 200 customers lets each one "connect Slack" by pasting their own incoming webhook URL into a settings field. Support tickets start arriving: customers who regenerate their webhook URL (Slack allows this) silently break the integration with no error on either side, and one customer's webhook URL was found posted in a public GitHub issue after they copy-pasted their whole settings page into a bug report.
contentSections.question: What's the structural cause of both problems?

options.label: The customers themselves are being careless
A raw webhook URL is a bearer secret with no way to detect regeneration or scope who can see it — the integration model itself invites this
Slack's webhook feature is fundamentally unreliable

feedback.carelessness: Individual mistakes happen, but a system that depends on 200 separate customers never mishandling a raw secret, and never being surprised by a silent regeneration, is a system that will produce this exact failure pattern reliably, regardless of how careful any individual customer is.
feedback.structural: Right. A webhook URL functions like an unrotatable, unrevoked-by-you API key handed directly to each customer to store and paste around — nothing in the model gives your tool visibility into whether it's still valid, and nothing prevents a customer from treating it like ordinary settings text rather than a secret.
feedback.unreliable: The webhook feature itself works exactly as designed and documented — it was never meant to be the multi-tenant customer-facing integration mechanism it's being stretched into here.

contentSections.mechanism: **A Slack app with OAuth is the mechanism built for exactly this case.** Each customer clicks 'Add to Slack,' goes through Slack's own authorization screen, and your tool receives a proper access token tied to that specific workspace — one your tool controls, can detect as revoked (Slack notifies your app), and never asks the customer to copy-paste around. The extra setup (registering the app, requesting scopes, building the OAuth callback) is the cost of solving a problem raw webhook URLs were never designed to solve.

contentSections.body: The concrete cost difference, honestly: an incoming webhook costs nothing beyond the five minutes to create it, and there's no ongoing Slack-side approval process for internal use. A Slack app is free to create and free to install into workspaces you or your customers control, but it does add real engineering surface — an OAuth flow, token storage (per-workspace, needs to be encrypted at rest, exactly like any other credential), and, if you ever want it listed in Slack's App Directory for public discovery, a review process with real requirements around security and scope justification. For a solo builder's own tool posting to their own channel, that's a lot of machinery to build for no benefit — the webhook is correctly the simpler, cheaper, entirely sufficient choice.

Reach for a Slack app only when the requirement is per-customer connection, reading Slack, or a persistent bot identity. Otherwise the five-minute webhook is the right answer, not a shortcut you'll regret.

title: Formatting a Message Someone Will Actually Read
description: The difference between a wall of text and a message that survives being read in three seconds on a phone — Block Kit structure, and what plain-text formatting can't do.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the difference between the text field and Block Kit structure
Compose a Slack message using headers, sections, and dividers appropriately
Recognize formatting choices that get skimmed past versus ones that get read

contentSections.title: The wall of text nobody reads

contentSections.body: A tool posts a genuinely useful daily summary to Slack — five paragraphs of plain text, all the numbers that matter buried in sentence three. Three weeks in, a teammate admits they haven't actually read one since day two. The information was correct. The format made it invisible.

contentSections.scenario:
Two versions of the same daily summary.

**A.** `{"text": "Daily report: 14 new signups, 3 churned, MRR now $8,200, up 2% from yesterday. 2 support tickets opened, both resolved. Site uptime 99.98%."}`

**B.** A Block Kit message with a header ("Daily Report — Feb 12"), a section with bolded key numbers laid out in a short list, a divider, then a smaller context line for the uptime figure.
contentSections.question: Both contain the same information. Why does B actually get read and A gets skimmed past?

options.label: B contains more information overall
B's structure lets someone find the number they care about without reading every word in order
A is technically invalid Slack formatting

feedback.more: Both convey identical information — nothing was added or removed. The difference is entirely about how it's laid out, not how much of it there is.
feedback.scan: Right. A dense paragraph forces a linear read to extract any single fact — find the MRR number, and you have to parse the whole sentence. Structured blocks let someone's eye land directly on the number they're checking for, which is how messages actually get consumed in a busy channel: skimmed, not read start to finish.
feedback.invalid: Plain text in the `text` field is perfectly valid Slack formatting — it just isn't the formatting that supports scanning.

contentSections.concept: **A Slack message is read the way a notification is read: in the two or three seconds before attention moves on.** The `text` field alone is a single string, rendered as one block of prose — Slack's mrkdwn subset supports bold, links, and simple lists inline, but everything still reads top to bottom as one paragraph. **Block Kit** is a structured JSON format — an array of typed blocks (`header`, `section`, `divider`, `context`) — that gives you actual visual hierarchy: a bold title, a short list of key numbers, a visually distinct secondary detail.

contentSections.body:
A minimal Block Kit structure for the same report:

```json
{
  "blocks": [
    { "type": "header", "text": { "type": "plain_text", "text": "Daily Report — Feb 12" } },
    { "type": "section", "text": { "type": "mrkdwn",
        "text": "*Signups:* 14  |  *Churned:* 3  |  *MRR:* $8,200 (+2%)" } },
    { "type": "divider" },
    { "type": "context", "elements": [
        { "type": "mrkdwn", "text": "Uptime 99.98% · 2 tickets opened, both resolved" } ] }
  ]
}
```

Still worth including a `text` field alongside `blocks` — it's the fallback shown in notification previews and by clients that can't render blocks, so it should carry a short plain-language summary even when the real formatting lives in `blocks`.
A message is skimmed, not read start to finish. Block Kit's visual hierarchy — header, key numbers, divider, secondary detail — is what makes the important fact findable in the first second.

contentSections.title: The line between structured and cluttered

contentSections.body: The failure mode on the other side is real too: a message with a header, three sections, two dividers, four context blocks and an image, for a notification that's really just "the build passed." More structure isn't automatically more readable.

contentSections.code:
// A CI tool's build-success notification:
blocks: [
  header("✅ Build Succeeded"),
  section("*Repository:* my-app"),
  divider(),
  section("*Branch:* main"),
  divider(),
  section("*Commit:* a1b2c3d"),
  divider(),
  section("*Duration:* 2m 14s"),
  divider(),
  section("*Triggered by:* deploy bot"),
  context("View full logs →")
]
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong here, given the message is just announcing a routine success?

options.label: This is technically invalid Block Kit and will fail to render
Five separate sections and four dividers for five short facts turns a routine notification into something that takes real effort to scan, which defeats the whole point of structuring it
Slack limits messages to 3 blocks maximum

feedback.invalid: This would render fine — Block Kit has no problem with this many blocks. The issue is legibility, not validity.
feedback.overstructured: Right. Five stacked sections with dividers between every single one makes a reader scroll and parse five separate visual chunks for information that fits comfortably in one or two lines. The one case this module opened with — a wall of undifferentiated text — has been replaced with the opposite failure: over-segmented structure that takes just as much effort to skim, for a routine event that arguably didn't need more than a single line at all.
feedback.limit3: Slack's actual block limit per message is much higher (50 blocks) — this isn't hitting any real platform limit, it's a design choice that happens to be a bad one.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A better version for a routine success: one section combining the key facts (`*my-app* · main · a1b2c3d · 2m 14s · <link|View logs>`), no dividers at all — dividers earn their place separating genuinely distinct groups of information, not every individual fact. Save the fuller structure (header, distinct sections, dividers) for messages where there's real heterogeneous content to separate — a build *failure* with an error excerpt, a stack trace snippet, and a set of suggested next steps, for instance, where those actually are three different kinds of information worth visually distinguishing.

contentSections.body: Structure earns its place when there's genuinely heterogeneous information to separate. A routine one-fact notification wants one clean line, not five sections and four dividers.

title: Rate Limits and Batching Instead of Spamming a Channel
description: Slack's real rate limits, what actually happens when a tool hits them, and the batching pattern that turns fifty separate pings into one message anyone will actually keep in the channel.

learningObjectives.text: State Slack's incoming webhook rate limit and what happens when it's exceeded
Design a batching window that groups related events into one message
Predict the human cost of an unbatched, high-frequency integration

contentSections.title: What the rate limit actually is

contentSections.body: A tool starts posting one Slack message per event during a busy hour — 80 messages in twenty minutes. Some of them silently never arrive. The channel members who didn't get muted mid-storm mute it themselves by the next morning.

contentSections.scenario: Slack's incoming webhooks are rate-limited per webhook URL — a documented limit on how many messages can be posted in a short window before Slack starts rejecting requests.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many messages per minute can a single incoming webhook sustain before hitting Slack's rate limit?
contentSections.actualValue: about 1 per second (roughly 60/minute), with bursts tolerated briefly
contentSections.explanation: Slack's documented guidance for incoming webhooks is roughly one message per second sustained, with some tolerance for short bursts above that before you start receiving `429 Too Many Requests` responses — the exact numbers have shifted over Slack's history and are worth checking against current docs before depending on them precisely, but the shape is consistent: this is not a limit a normal daily-summary tool will ever approach, and it's trivially easy to blow through with an unbatched high-frequency integration (one message per scraped item, one message per log line, one message per webhook event received from somewhere else).

contentSections.body: What actually happens past the limit: Slack returns a `429` response with a `Retry-After` header telling you how long to wait. A well-behaved integration respects that header and retries later; a naive one either drops the message silently (if the error isn't checked) or retries immediately in a loop, which can make the situation worse. Either way, **the technical rate limit is rarely the real problem** — a solo builder's tool posting 60 messages a minute has usually already lost the channel's attention long before Slack's infrastructure starts pushing back.
Slack's own rate limit (roughly one message per second) is generous for normal use and trivially easy to blow through with an unbatched, per-event integration.

contentSections.title: Batching: one message instead of fifty

contentSections.body: The fix isn't slowing down to stay under the rate limit — it's asking why fifty separate messages were the right shape in the first place, when the reader almost certainly wanted one summary.

contentSections.scenario: A price-tracking tool posts one Slack message per price drop detected. During a site-wide sale, 43 tracked products drop in price within the same ten-minute scraping run, producing 43 separate messages in the channel in quick succession.
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong here, beyond the raw message count?

options.label: 43 messages will definitely exceed Slack's rate limit
43 separate messages for one underlying event (a sale) forces the reader to reconstruct the summary themselves by scrolling through them all
Slack messages can't be posted that close together in time

feedback.ratelimit: 43 messages over ten minutes is well within the documented rate limit — this isn't a Slack infrastructure problem at all.
feedback.reconstruct: Right. The real cost is entirely human: someone opening the channel now has to scroll through 43 messages to get what should have been one glance's worth of information — 'a sale is happening, 43 tracked products dropped, here's the list' — and every one of those 43 messages is also a notification, if notifications are on, which is its own cost.
feedback.timing: There's no such restriction — messages can be posted arbitrarily close together, within the rate limit. The problem isn't a technical one at all.

contentSections.mechanism: **The underlying event here isn't '43 price drops' — it's 'a sale happened, and here's what it affected.'** Posting one message per drop treats the symptom (individual data points) as the event, when the actual event a human would care about is the aggregate. Batching — collecting related events over a short window and posting one combined summary — fixes both the rate-limit risk and, more importantly, the actual reading experience.

contentSections.problem: Redesign the price-drop tool to batch instead of posting one message per drop.

steps.label: Pick a batching window
steps.work: Instead of posting immediately on each detected drop, accumulate detected drops into an in-memory (or database-backed) list for a fixed window — say, the duration of one scraping run (ten minutes), or a rolling 5-minute window if drops are detected continuously.
steps.why: The window should match how the tool actually generates events — batching by scraping run is natural here since drops are already discovered in discrete batches, not a continuous stream.

steps.label: Post once, at the end of the window
steps.work: After the scraping run finishes, if the accumulated list has one or more drops, post a single message: a header ('Price Drops — 43 products'), then either the full list (if short) or a summarized top few plus a count ('...and 38 more, view all →' linking to a dashboard).
steps.why: One message per window, not per event, regardless of how many events occurred — this is what actually caps the message count independent of how busy any given run turns out to be.

steps.label: Handle the zero-events case by not posting at all
steps.work: If the window produced no drops, send nothing — no 'no drops this run' message.
steps.why: A batching window with nothing to report shouldn't itself become a new source of noise. Silence when nothing happened is the correct behavior for most notification tools, not a message confirming nothing happened.

steps.label: Keep a genuinely urgent case unbatched, deliberately
steps.work: If the tool also detects something time-sensitive — say, a tracked item selling out entirely, not just dropping price — that might reasonably bypass the batch window and post immediately, as a deliberate, documented exception.
steps.why: Batching is the default because most events aren't individually urgent, not a rule with no exceptions — the exceptions should be few, and consciously chosen, not accidental.

faded.problem: Now design batching for a different tool: a webhook handler that receives one event per row updated in an external spreadsheet integration, and currently posts one Slack message per row.

blanks.prompt: What's a reasonable batching window for events arriving continuously throughout the day, rather than in discrete runs?
blanks.answer: a short rolling window, e.g. collect events for 1-2 minutes then flush a summary
blanks.why: Continuous event streams (unlike the scraping tool's discrete runs) need a time-based window rather than a natural batch boundary — short enough that updates still feel timely, long enough to actually catch bursts of related changes.

blanks.prompt: What should the single batched message contain if 15 rows were updated in one window?
blanks.answer: a count and a short summary or list of the changes, not all 15 individually detailed
accept: a summary with the count and key details, not 15 separate entries
blanks.why: Same principle as the price-drop example — the batched message should read as one coherent summary, not 15 compressed-but-still-separate mini-messages stacked in one post.

blanks.prompt: What should happen if zero rows were updated in a given window?
blanks.answer: nothing gets posted
blanks.why: An empty window isn't itself news, and confirming 'nothing happened' every couple minutes would just become the new source of noise this whole redesign was meant to eliminate.

blanks.prompt: Name one kind of update to this spreadsheet that might reasonably justify bypassing the batch window entirely.
blanks.answer: a row marked as something urgent, e.g. a status changed to 'critical' or a flagged error row
blanks.why: As with the price tool's sold-out case, a genuine exception should be deliberate and rare — most row updates aren't individually time-sensitive, but a specific, well-defined subset might be.

contentSections.procedure: **Accumulate over a window, post one summary, stay silent on empty windows, carve out deliberate exceptions for genuine urgency.** The window's length is the one thing that has to be tuned to the actual tool — matched to how events naturally arrive, not copied wholesale from a different integration.

contentSections.body: Batching isn't primarily a rate-limit defense — it's recognizing that the real event a human cares about is usually the aggregate, not each individual data point.

title: Handling a Failed Send Without Losing the Result
description: Why a Slack post failing shouldn't mean the underlying work is lost — persisting the result before attempting delivery, and retrying delivery separately from redoing the work.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why coupling result computation and result delivery is risky
Design a handler that persists a result before attempting to deliver it
Distinguish a delivery failure from a work failure and respond to each appropriately

contentSections.title: The result that only ever existed in a failed POST

contentSections.body: A tool spends 40 seconds calling an AI API to generate a detailed report, then POSTs the result to Slack. Slack's servers happen to be having a rough five minutes; the POST times out. The 40 seconds of real, paid-for work is gone — nothing wrote it down anywhere before trying to send it.

contentSections.scenario: The code above does, in sequence: generate the report (expensive), then `fetch(webhookUrl, {...})` to post it, with no error handling around the fetch call beyond letting an exception propagate and crash the job.
contentSections.question: What's the actual design flaw, independent of whether Slack itself is reliable?

options.label: The AI API call should have a longer timeout
The result of real, completed work exists nowhere except inside a network request that might fail for reasons entirely outside the tool's control
Slack webhooks are inherently too unreliable to depend on

feedback.timeout: The AI call's timeout isn't the issue here — the report generation already succeeded by the time the problem occurs; the failure is entirely in what happens after.
feedback.coupling: Right. The 40 seconds of real work produced a real result, and that result's only representation anywhere is the in-memory variable about to be POSTed. If the POST fails for any reason — Slack's servers, a network blip, a bad webhook URL — that result is gone, full stop, with no way to recover it short of redoing the expensive work.
feedback.unreliable: Slack's incoming webhooks are generally reliable, but 'generally reliable' still means occasional failures happen — the design flaw is building a system with zero tolerance for an occasional, expected kind of failure, not that Slack specifically is untrustworthy.

contentSections.mechanism: **Delivery failure and work failure are two different things, and this code treats them as one.** The work (generating the report) succeeded. The delivery (posting to Slack) failed. Losing the completed work because the *delivery* step failed is exactly backwards — the expensive, hard-to-redo part succeeded; the cheap, easy-to-retry part is what broke.

contentSections.body: The fix follows directly: **persist the result before attempting delivery, not after.** A row in a `notifications` table — the content, the intended destination, a status field starting at `pending` — written the moment the real work finishes, before the Slack POST is even attempted. If the POST succeeds, update the status to `delivered`. If it fails, the status stays `pending` (or moves to `failed`), but the actual content is safe in the database regardless of what happened on the network. A separate, simple retry process — even just 'try any `pending` notifications again on the next scheduled run' — can pick it up later without redoing the expensive report generation at all.
A delivery failure should never cost you completed work. Persist the result the moment it exists, before attempting to send it anywhere.

Persisting the result solves losing it. It doesn't automatically solve the next problem: a naive retry loop can now post the same report to Slack three times because the first two 'failures' actually succeeded, just slowly, and the retry logic didn't know that.

contentSections.question: This retries on failure, which sounds right. What's actually broken about how it decides something failed?

options.label: It doesn't wait long enough between retries
A slow-but-successful request that merely times out client-side throws an exception too, so this retries requests that may have actually already succeeded, risking duplicate posts
fetch() can't be used inside a try/catch block

feedback.wait: The wait duration is a minor tuning detail, not the core problem — even with a perfectly tuned backoff, the deeper issue remains.
feedback.ambiguous: Right. A client-side timeout means 'I stopped waiting for a response,' not 'the server didn't process the request.' Slack may well have received and posted the message just before the client gave up — in which case retrying sends a second, genuinely duplicate message, for a delivery that already succeeded.
feedback.syntax: This is syntactically fine — try/catch around an async fetch call is a completely standard, valid pattern. The bug is in the logic, not the syntax.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The general fix mirrors idempotency from the webhooks module: a durable, unique identifier per notification, checked before each retry attempt actually re-sends. For Slack specifically, one practical mitigation is including a distinguishing marker (like a timestamp or notification ID) in the message content itself, so an accidental duplicate is at least visible and traceable rather than silently identical — full request-level idempotency (a true 'only ever post this once' guarantee) isn't something Slack's incoming webhook API provides, unlike some payment APIs' idempotency-key support, so the practical mitigation here is being conservative about what counts as a genuine failure worth retrying, not assuming every thrown exception means nothing happened.

contentSections.body: Worth being honest about the actual scope of this problem: for most solo tools, an occasional duplicate Slack message from a rare timeout-during-retry edge case is a minor annoyance, not a correctness disaster the way a duplicate charge would be (module two's subject). The response should be proportionate — persisting results so nothing is *lost* is close to always worth the small amount of code it takes; building elaborate delivery-deduplication machinery for a notification channel, where the worst case is someone sees the same Slack message twice, usually isn't worth the engineering time it would cost, unless the tool has a specific reason duplicates would be genuinely harmful.

Persist results unconditionally — that's cheap and always worth it. Retry delivery carefully, aware that a timeout doesn't prove failure — but don't over-engineer duplicate protection past what a notification channel's real stakes justify.

title: Letting People Configure Where Their Results Go
description: Moving from one hardcoded webhook URL to letting each user choose their own destination — a settings model, and what has to change once that URL is user-supplied rather than developer-set.

learningObjectives.text: Design a settings model for user-configurable notification destinations
Identify what changes about trust and validation once a webhook URL is user-supplied
Handle a user's destination becoming invalid gracefully

contentSections.title: From one hardcoded URL to a setting

contentSections.body: A tool that worked fine with one hardcoded webhook URL in an environment variable gets its first request: "can I get my results in my own Slack instead of yours?" The honest answer requires more than swapping which URL the code posts to.

contentSections.scenario:
Two ways of letting users choose their own Slack destination.

**A.** Add a `slackWebhookUrl` text field to the user's settings page. They paste in a URL they generated themselves from their own Slack workspace's incoming webhook settings.

**B.** Add an 'Add to Slack' OAuth button. Clicking it sends them through Slack's own authorization flow, and the tool receives and stores an access token for their workspace.
contentSections.question: For a tool where most users are non-technical and won't know how to create a Slack incoming webhook themselves, which approach is more appropriate as the primary path?

options.label: A — it's simpler to build
B — it doesn't require the user to know what an incoming webhook even is
Either works equally well regardless of the audience

feedback.a: Simpler to build, yes — but that simplicity is shifted onto the user, who now has to navigate Slack's own admin settings, understand what an incoming webhook is, generate one, and correctly paste a long URL without a typo. For a non-technical audience, that's a real adoption barrier, not a minor inconvenience.
feedback.b: Right. The OAuth flow puts the complexity on your side (building it once) instead of on every individual user (learning Slack's admin interface each time). 'Add to Slack' is a button most users already recognize the pattern of, from other tools.
feedback.either: They produce a similar end result technically, but the actual user experience — and therefore adoption rate — differs meaningfully depending on how technical the audience is. This isn't a neutral choice.

contentSections.concept: **Who has to do the harder setup work is a real design decision, not a neutral implementation detail.** Option A (paste-your-own-URL) is faster to build and completely reasonable for a technical audience (developers, ops teams) who already know what a webhook is. Option B (OAuth) costs more engineering time up front but removes that burden from every user, which usually matters more the broader and less technical the audience is.

contentSections.body: For a tool where letting users paste their own webhook URL is the right call (a technical audience, or a fast MVP before investing in full OAuth), the settings model itself is simple: a `notificationSettings` table or column, keyed by user, storing the destination URL, whether notifications are enabled, and — worth including from the start — which categories of event the user wants sent there, if the tool produces more than one kind of notification. Not every user wants every event type in the same channel, and building that as a single on/off toggle now is much cheaper than retrofitting per-category control later once users are already relying on the all-or-nothing version.
Who has to do the setup work — you once, or every user individually — is a real product decision. Match it to how technical the audience actually is.

contentSections.title: What changes once the URL is user-supplied

contentSections.body: The moment a webhook URL comes from a settings field instead of an environment variable you control, every assumption from earlier in this module about 'the URL is a trusted destination' needs a second look.

contentSections.scenario: A tool now lets users paste their own Slack incoming webhook URL into a settings field, which the backend then POSTs results to.
contentSections.question: Select every consideration below that genuinely becomes relevant once the destination URL is user-supplied rather than developer-controlled.

items.label: The backend should validate the URL is actually a Slack webhook URL pattern, not an arbitrary attacker-supplied endpoint the server would blindly POST to (a server-side request forgery risk)
A user's webhook URL might become invalid later (regenerated, workspace removed the integration) and the tool needs to handle that gracefully rather than failing silently forever
The stored URL should be treated as sensitive, similar to any other credential, not logged in plaintext or exposed in a public API response
Block Kit formatting needs to work differently depending on which user's URL is being posted to

explanation.ssrf: This is a real, specific new risk: your server is now making outbound requests to a URL supplied by an untrusted user, which is the textbook shape of an SSRF vulnerability if the destination isn't validated as actually being a Slack webhook endpoint rather than, say, an internal service address.
explanation.invalid: Genuinely new — with one hardcoded URL you control, you'd notice it breaking immediately. With hundreds of user-supplied URLs, individual ones going stale is now a routine, expected occurrence that needs its own handling (surfacing it to that specific user, not failing silently).
explanation.encryption: A pasted-in webhook URL is a bearer secret exactly like any other credential the moment it's user-supplied and stored — it deserves the same handling (not logged, not exposed) as an API key would.
explanation.formatting: Block Kit's structure and behavior don't depend on which URL a message is posted to — this isn't a real consideration introduced by user-supplied destinations at all.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the three real considerations: **user-supplied input crossing into a trust boundary always needs revalidation, not just a data-model change.** The URL field looks identical whether it's hardcoded or user-supplied, but the trust assumptions your code was making about it are completely different, and code written for the hardcoded case will quietly carry those assumptions forward unless someone deliberately revisits them.

contentSections.body: Practically: validate that a submitted URL matches Slack's actual webhook URL pattern (`https://hooks.slack.com/services/...`) before ever storing or POSTing to it — this alone closes most of the SSRF concern cheaply. For staleness, wrap delivery attempts in error handling that, on a repeated failure specifically matching 'webhook no longer valid' (Slack returns a distinct error for a revoked webhook), flips that user's notification setting to disabled and surfaces a visible notice in their settings UI, rather than silently retrying forever against a destination that will never work again.

A user-supplied destination needs everything a developer-controlled one didn't: format validation against SSRF, credential-grade storage, and graceful handling of a destination that quietly goes stale.

title: Lab — Send Your Tool's Results to Slack Properly
description: Take a real (or realistic) result your tool produces and deliver it to Slack the way this module actually argued for: well-formatted, batched if appropriate, and never lost to a failed send.

learningObjectives.text: Implement a Slack delivery using Block Kit formatting appropriate to the content
Persist a result before attempting delivery and handle a failed send without data loss
Justify a batching decision (or the deliberate absence of one) for the specific content being sent

contentSections.body: This is the module's whole point assembled into one integration. A Slack delivery that reads well, doesn't spam, and never silently loses a result is the difference between a channel people keep and one they mute by the end of the week.

contentSections.title: A Slack integration you'd actually keep unmuted
contentSections.brief:
Pick a real piece of output your tool produces (or would produce) — a scrape result, a daily summary, an error alert, a report. If nothing fits, use this concrete stand-in: a script that checks 2-3 hardcoded URLs for content changes (reusing module one's scheduling and module two's concepts if it helps) and reports what it found.

Build the whole path: choose the right integration type, format it to be skimmable, batch it if the content warrants it, and never lose the result if the send fails.
contentSections.deliverable: A working Slack delivery — an incoming webhook is sufficient unless your tool genuinely needs a full app — that posts a well-formatted, appropriately batched message, backed by a persisted record that survives a failed send.

stages.title: Set up the webhook and a first plain message
stages.instructions: Create an incoming webhook for a Slack channel you control (or a test workspace), and get one plain-text message posting successfully from your code. Confirm you can see it arrive in the channel.
stages.checkpoint: A real message from your code has actually appeared in a real Slack channel.

stages.title: Format it with Block Kit
stages.instructions: Rewrite the message using Block Kit — a header, a section with the key facts laid out for scanning, and a divider or context block only if there's genuinely more than one kind of information to separate. Deliberately avoid over-structuring a small number of routine facts.
stages.checkpoint: You can explain, in one sentence, why each block you included earns its place — not just that it's technically valid.

stages.title: Persist before sending
stages.instructions: Add a record (a database row, or a local file if you're keeping this lightweight) that captures the fully-composed message content before the send is attempted, with a status field. Update the status after the send succeeds or fails. Deliberately break the webhook URL temporarily and confirm the content survives the failed send.
stages.checkpoint: You've caused a real send failure on purpose and confirmed the content is still sitting there afterward, recoverable.

stages.title: Decide, explicitly, on batching
stages.instructions: If your tool's content naturally produces multiple related events (several results from one run, several changes detected), implement a batching window per lesson three. If it genuinely doesn't (a single daily summary, one alert type that's rare by nature), write a short, explicit justification for why batching doesn't apply here — 'no batching needed' should be a decision, not an omission.
stages.checkpoint: You can state, specifically, either your batching window's boundary and why you chose it, or why this content doesn't need batching at all.

rubric.criterion: The integration type matches the actual requirement
rubric.meets: An incoming webhook is used unless there's a genuine documented reason (per-user destinations, reading Slack back) that requires a full app.

rubric.criterion: Formatting is deliberate, not maximal or minimal by default
rubric.meets: Block Kit structure is used where content is genuinely heterogeneous, and a single clean line is used where it isn't — you can justify the choice either way.

rubric.criterion: A result is never lost to a failed send
rubric.meets: You've demonstrated, with a real forced failure, that the content survives and is recoverable after a failed delivery attempt.

rubric.criterion: Batching is a decision, not an accident
rubric.meets: Either a working batching window with a stated, sensible boundary, or an explicit written justification for why this content doesn't need one.

rubric.criterion: The message is actually skimmable
rubric.meets: A person unfamiliar with the tool could glance at the posted message and extract the key fact in a few seconds.

rubric.criterion: The whole path survives being explained cold
rubric.meets: You could describe integration choice → format → persist → send → batch decision to someone else without looking at the code, in under two minutes.

contentSections.body: Right integration type, skimmable formatting, deliberate batching, never-lose-the-result. Four decisions, each one the fix for a specific way Slack integrations quietly become the channel everyone mutes.
